paragraphs.text: Father Dorotheus v Fear the Lord and keep His commandments, which strengthen you in all your affairs, so that there is none like your works... Do not fear Satan if you fear the Lord, for your fear of God gives you authority over Satan [38].
Hermas St. Clement of Alexandria sees that the Lord often speaks and threatens before He disciplines, so that man may turn back from his evil.

v The Lord often speaks before He carries out the work (the discipline). He says: "I will spend My arrows upon them; they shall be burnt with hunger, and devoured with burning heat, and with bitter destruction. I will also send the teeth of beasts upon them, with the poison of serpents of the earth. The sword without, and terror within, shall destroy" (Deut 32:23-25). This does not mean that the Divine Spirit becomes angry, as some suppose. He often shows restraint along with encouragement, and shows us what we ought to do. He uses this effective means, which lies in stirring up fear in us, so that we do not commit sin [39].
St. Clement of Alexandria Unjust anger cannot be justified, for the sure effect of anger causes its downfall [19].

v In truth, just as madmen and fools do not notice this when they cast themselves into the abyss, so it is with those who lose their gentleness and are struck by anger. This is why the wise man, who wishes to expose the destruction of this intoxication (anger), says: "The wrath of man turns the scale of the balance to his own destruction." Observe how he binds himself in slavery to the work of this passion, destructive in its weight [40].

v Anger is a ravening beast, a violent and raging beast. Let us then prescribe for ourselves a soothing draught taken from Holy Scripture, and say: "Why (how) is he proud who is dust and ashes?" (Sir 10:9), the weight of his anger destroys him (cf. Sir 1:19)... Nothing is more shameful, nothing is uglier than a face inflamed with anger. When you stir up mud, you smell a foul odor. And when a soul is disturbed by passion, it becomes exceedingly foul [41].

v The passion of anger is ravenous, fiercer than any flame. For this reason we need to hasten very quickly to prevent the flame, and not allow it to blaze up on high. For this sickness becomes the cause of many evils. It brings down whole houses, dissolves old friendships, and causes calamities that cannot be remedied in a short time. It was said: "The wrath of man turns the scale of the balance to his own destruction" [42].
St. John Chrysostom The long-suffering man bears patiently until the right time, and afterward joy returns to him with power [20].

Ben Sirach distinguishes between a man who is wronged and so becomes angry and rages, and another who falls under wrong and endures with long-suffering. The first, although his anger rests on a wrong that has befallen him, is burdened by his own anger, and so he falls, even if he thinks he is justifying himself. The second endures for a time in silence, and then joy returns to him, and many bear witness for him while he is silent and does not defend himself.
He holds back his words until the right time, and the lips of many tell of his understanding [21].

entries.section: 3. Wisdom and the divine commandment

paragraphs.text: 31 In the treasures of wisdom are the parables of knowledge, 32 but to the sinner the worship of God is an abomination. 33 My son, if you desire wisdom, keep the commandments, and the Lord will give her to you. 34 For wisdom and instruction are the fear of the Lord, and that which pleases Him 35 is faith and meekness, and He will fill him who has them with treasures. 36 Do not disobey the fear of the Lord, and do not come to Him with a double heart. 37 Be not a hypocrite in the sight of men, and keep watch over your lips. 38 Exalt not yourself, lest you fall, and bring dishonor upon your soul, 39 and the Lord reveal your secrets, and cast you down in the midst of the congregation, 40 because you came not to the fear of the Lord, but your heart is full of deceit.
In the treasures of wisdom are the parables of knowledge, but godliness is an abomination to the sinner [22].
If godliness is an abomination to the sinner, how much more can the enemy of good, the devil, not bear it, and so he rages against the godly; yet he has no authority to harm them.
v If (the demons) had authority, they would not hesitate to use it, but would practice evil at once, since this is their aim, especially against us.

Behold, we are gathered together speaking against them, and they know it, that the more we advance, the weaker they become. If they had authority, they would not have allowed any of us Christians to live, for the service of God is an abomination to the sinner (cf. Sir 1:22). But since they have no authority, they harm themselves, for they cannot carry out anything of what they threaten. This obliges us not to fear them [43].
St. Athanasius the Apostolic If you desire wisdom, keep the commandments, and the Lord will give her to you [23].

The philosophy discovered by the Gentiles is the product of human understanding, but Holy Scripture proclaims that understanding is from God Himself, who gives it to him who believes in His commandments.
v Do not forsake the commandment of the Lord, but keep what you have received, neither adding to it nor taking away from it [44].
The Didache (the Teaching of the Twelve Disciples)
v I have been absorbed in the commandments that You gave me, and meditated on them with wisdom; I believed in them until I kept them.
Grant me, then, wisdom by teaching me goodness, discipline and knowledge.
This petition agrees with the saying: "My son, if you desire wisdom, keep the commandments, and the Lord will give her to you" (cf. Sir 1:23).

St. Didymus the Blind v The (first) Psalm draws for us the way of virtue with knowledge and skill. Turning away from evil is the beginning of good. If you ask from the beginning for the perfection of virtue, you will draw back before you start; but the Psalm prepares the way for us to face it with courage.

And I believe that growth in the love of God is like the ladder that the blessed Jacob once saw, which was on the earth on one side and on the other side was reaching toward the life of virtue, where a man begins by climbing the first rungs of the ladder, and after that rises to a higher rung with deliberation and patience, until he reaches what human nature can attain.
So, by climbing the first rungs of the ladder, we rise above the earth, to live the life that God wills for us.

And the beginning of progress is to keep away from evil, where such keeping away is easy, as in: "You shall not kill, you shall not commit adultery, you shall not steal" (Ex 20:13-15); this does not require any positive work. But when we are required to keep that commandment: "Love your neighbor as yourself," "Sell what you have and give to the poor" (Mt 19:21), "Whoever compels you to go one mile, go with him two" (Mt 5:41), these works are done by the wrestler who has tested his strength by divine wisdom, who through small works leads us to perfection.
For he sets before us three things that we must avoid: walking in the counsel of the wicked, standing in the way of sinners, and sitting in the seat of the scornful.

This order begins with making the decision and then carrying out the beginning, here in pure thought. For the foundation of the works of the flesh springs from purity of heart; adultery begins in the lustful soul and ends in adultery of the body. Therefore the Lord said: "That which defiles a man comes out of the heart" (cf. Mt 15:18) [45].
St. Basil the Great Origen sees that wisdom begins with upright conduct, or keeping the divine commandment.

v If anyone meditates in the law of the Lord day and night (Ps 1:2), and is like the mouth of the righteous that speaks wisdom (Ps 37:30), he will be able to ask with care and find. So it will be, on condition that he asks in a sound manner, and by his asking knocks at the door of wisdom, to ask God to open it to him, and is made worthy to receive by the Holy Spirit the word of wisdom and the word of knowledge, and becomes a companion of the wisdom of Solomon [46].

v "I have stretched out my hand, and no man regarded" (Prov 1:24). It is reasonable that he said that He (God) stretches out His words in his heart (the heart of Solomon)... because God gave him a large heart.
He is able to explain, in brief, what is stated in the mysteries, within the broad, harmonious and confirmed teachings of Holy Scripture, since he has a large heart.

Therefore, in agreement with the teachings of the wise Solomon, it is necessary for the person who desires to know wisdom to begin with training in conduct, so that he may understand what is written: "Do you long for wisdom? Keep the commandments, and it will be given to you by God" [47].
Origen v Wisdom is good; it fills with joy those who possess her, and brings down those who do not practice (the commandments).

But what does Holy Scripture say? The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom (cf. Sir 1:12). Who does not love to reign? And in the Psalms there is the counsel of the Spirit: "Now therefore, O you kings, be wise; be instructed, you judges of the earth. Serve the Lord with fear, and rejoice with trembling." This is the reason for Paul's saying: "Work out your own salvation with fear and trembling" (Phil 2:12). And we read: "If you desire wisdom, observe justice, and the Lord will grant her to you [48]."

v You must order your life by the commandments of God, which we receive to help us walk the good life, beginning with godly fear, for "the fear of the Lord is the head of wisdom" (Prov 1:7), while human pride breaks and weakens [49].

The commandments are those that concern the good, that is, bring the good; and the good is faith without doubt. Hence wisdom is the reward of pure faith. And the reward will be what eye has not seen [50].

St. Augustine v People are commonly called "wise," with a misuse of the word "wise." For the wise are not those who study the sayings and writings of the early wise Fathers, but those whose souls are rational, able to distinguish between what is good and what is evil. They avoid what is evil and harmful to the soul, and wisely take care of what is good and profitable to the soul and practice it with great thanksgiving to God. These alone are truly those whom we should call "wise" [51].
St. Anthony the Great v The knowledge of goodness is not enough for blessedness for him who does not put goodness into practice; true godliness toward God is the beginning of knowledge [52].
St. Didymus the Blind For the fear of the Lord is wisdom and instruction, and that which pleases Him is faith and meekness [24].

v In truth the divinity is not angry, as some suppose; rather, when God uses many threats, He does this as an appeal, showing mankind the things that will come to pass. These are measures that are certainly good; He plants fear to keep us from sin. "The fear of the Lord drives away sin, and he who has no fear cannot be justified." The punishment that God imposes is not from anger but from justice; and he who neglects justice makes no progress [53].
St. Clement of Alexandria Do not disobey the fear of the Lord, and do not come to Him with a double heart [25].

An undivided mind: to enjoy the holy fear of the Lord, which gives wisdom, it is fitting for the believer to keep the divine commandments, for they support his faith in God, and also grant him to be adorned with meekness, so that he does not fall into arrogance even toward unbelievers [27]. And on the other hand, he clings to God with all his heart, without duplicity.

As he speaks of wisdom and its connection with the divine commandment, he calls us to the life of simplicity as the key to obedience to the commandment, warning us against the double heart. If simplicity directs our hearts to the way of truth without deviation, the double heart makes man lose his aim, so that he gives an hour to the Lord and an hour to amusement and temporal pleasures.
As St. Gregory, bishop of Nyssa, speaks of the virtues, he puts simplicity of heart first, which is the opposite of duplicity of heart, saying:

v Concerning the elements of virtue, which kind of them it is fitting to regard as the greatest, and which of them we need to practice more than the others, this is their order; these things cannot be put into words. For they all have the same dignity, and lead the one who practices them to the heights by way of each one of them.

For simplicity opens the way to obedience, and obedience to faith, and faith to hope, and hope to righteousness (justice), and righteousness to service, and service to humility. By this is achieved the kindness that leads to grace, and grace to love, and love to prayer. Thus every virtue depends on the other virtues. And the virtues lead us to the summit of what we desire. Just as the crown of evil leads its friends to ever-increasing evil... Besides this, it is necessary for us to continue steadfastly in prayer (Rom 12:12). For prayer is like the leader of the chorus of the virtues [54].

St. Gregory, bishop of Nyssa Let us follow God with our whole being, or with all our heart and all our mind: "You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, and with all your soul, and with all your strength, and with all your mind" (Lk 10:27).

v These alone receive within them the greatness of the commandment and its priority: not only do they love the Lord their God, but they set themselves to accomplish this by three conditions; that is, with all their heart they hold within them the perfection of this love, its thoughts and its works; and with all their soul, that is, they are ready to give it up for the service of God who created all things, when the spreading of His word requires it; for God is loved with all the soul when no part of the soul is held back outside the keeping of the faith; and they love Him with all the mind, so that they think of nothing and speak of nothing but the divine things [55].

Origen v I believe that the wise man counsels divided persons, likening them to those who approach the way of God, when he says: "Do not come to the Lord with two hearts," but draw near to His way as one who sows and another who reaps [56].

St. Isaac the Syrian v The virtuous life is truly the source and root of wisdom, just as iniquity has folly as its source. I say this because the boaster and the slave of lust is taken captive by these vices as the fruit of lack of wisdom... Every sin begins with a lack of wisdom, just as the virtuous person who fears God is the wisest of all. For this reason the wise man says: "The fear of the Lord is the head of wisdom" (Prov 1:7). If the fear of the Lord is to be wise, and the evildoer does not possess this fear, then he is truly stripped of wisdom, and he who is deprived of wisdom is truly the most foolish of all [57].

St. John Chrysostom v It is fitting for the Christian to think thus of his heavenly calling, and that his life be worthy of the gospel of Christ (Phil 1:27). It is fitting that the Christian not be of a double mind (Lk 12:29), nor be distracted from remembering God and His purposes and His judgments [58].
St. Basil the Great Be not a hypocrite in the sight of men, and keep watch over your lips [26].

It was said of the pride of the hypocrite that it lifts him up as if to heaven; with his arrogant thought he seems as one who leads himself to the heavenly life. In hypocrisy he thinks that his head has reached the clouds, for he thinks that his thinking mind is equal to the merits of the saints who went before him.

v Hypocrisy is hateful to God and abhorred by men; it brings no reward, and is of no use at all for the salvation of the soul, but rather destroys it. If someone flees into hypocrisy so that his matter may not be discovered, it is only for a time, for it does not last long; rather, everything is revealed, and brings shame upon its owner. Thus he is like an ugly woman whose outward adornment, put on her by artificial means, is stripped from her. Hypocrisy, then, is foreign to the saints, since it is impossible for anything of what we do or say to escape the eyes of the divinity, for it was said: "There is nothing covered that shall not be revealed, neither hid that shall not be known" (Lk 12:2). If all our words and works will be revealed on the day of judgment, then hypocrisy is wearisome and without profit. It is fitting for us to be proved as true worshippers who serve God with sincere and open countenances [59].

St. Cyril the Great v There may be one who gives his alms before men yet avoids making a show of it, and there is also one who does not give it before men yet boasts of it in secret. For God does not reward almsgiving according to how it is done, whether before men or not, but according to the intention of the one who does it [60].

v Everyone sees the thief, "hypocrisy," carrying everything before his eyes, and he rejoices in it! What a new kind of robbery, which attracts people and delights them while they are being robbed! [61]

St. John Chrysostom v What is the place of the hypocrite (Job 20:9) but the heart of his flatterers? For he rests in the place where he finds those who love him... But as long as he lives, he does not cease to teach his followers the same things that he practices, and through the boldness of his sinful way he begets others also in the likeness of his own vain deceit.
v Hypocrites appear fruitful and green in the eyes of their fellow creatures, but in the sight of the hidden Judge they appear fruitless and withered.
Pope Gregory (the Great)
Do not exalt yourself, lest you fall, and bring dishonor upon your soul.
And the Lord will reveal your secrets, and strike you down in the midst of the congregation, because you truly did not come to the fear of the Lord, and your heart is full of deceit [27].
Wisdom is a free gift that He offers to the humble; He offers it without partiality, and gives it to those who enjoy the fear of the Lord and take care to keep His commandments [27].
v Hate greatness, for it is the fruit full of death.
For Adam ate of it in Eden, and it gave him death.
And by it Satan fell from the beginning. By it the house of Adam fell from Paradise.
There is nothing with God so vile and hateful as the love of greatness, and him who exalts himself in pride.

St. Jacob of Serugh v Observe these proud and reckless people; observe the ox as it is prepared for slaughter, left to roam in freedom, destroying what it wishes, until the day of its slaughter... Holy Scripture points to it in another place as a sacrifice, and that it is left to an evil freedom (Prov 7:22) [62].

St. Augustine v Satan fell from his heavenly rank because of his pride; therefore he always does all he can to make fall all who wish to advance toward God with all their hearts, using the same means by which he himself fell, I mean greatness and the love of vainglory. By this and the like he fights us, in the hope of drawing us away from God...

What moved our Lord Jesus Christ to lay aside His garments, and gird Himself with a towel, and pour water into a basin, and wash the feet of those who were beneath Him (Jn 13:4 etc.), if not to teach us humility?! He showed us humility by the example He gave. Therefore those who wish to return to their first rank will not be able to do so except by humility. For pride is the cause of the fall from heaven in the beginning.
And so he who lacks deep humility, from all the heart and mind and spirit and body, does not inherit the Kingdom of God [63].

v Many have lived a long time as monks and virgins, and have not learned how to acquire purity. This is because they despise the teaching of their fathers and follow the desires of their own hearts. Therefore the evil spirits that destroy souls gained mastery over them, wounding them night and day with their unseen arrows, and giving them peace nowhere; rather they occupy their hearts now with pride, and now with vainglory and evil jealousy and slander and anger and fury and quarrels and many other passions. These have their portion with the five foolish virgins, for they passed their time in folly, and did not bridle their tongues, nor keep their eyes pure, nor keep their bodies from lusts or their hearts from impurities and the like [64].
St. Anthony the Great Inspired by Sirach 1

entries.section: Let me possess You, O wisdom of the eternal God!

paragraphs.text: v You are the wisdom of God, Creator of heaven and earth!
You are the wise One, greatly to be feared, sitting upon Your throne!
Who, of the heavenly orders or of men, can search out the mysteries of Your creation?!
Who can search out Your nature?
You are the wisdom of God; You came down to me that I might possess You, and become wise through You.
You are the Giver of wisdom and of every blessing; You have become a gift to me. I possess You within me and I cherish You!
v You gave me reason together with freedom of will so that I might contemplate the works of Your love; but when I stood helpless, You came down to me to dwell in my depths!
You came down to me to carry me in Yourself, and to prepare for me a place in Your heavens.
I meet You face to face, and my insight remains in amazement.
I depart to Paradise, and enjoy the eternal glories and their mysteries, without ceasing!
v My soul blesses You, who have given me the instinct of holy fear.
As I come to know You, Your holy fear is fixed in me, and my depths are glorified by Your dwelling in them.
I glory in You, my joy and the gladness of my heart!
Your fear leads me on the journey of my sojourn until the day of my departure from the world.
Your fear joins me to the orders of the heavenly ones, and I praise You with them with fear and trembling.
Your fear turns the dry wilderness of my heart into a paradise full of the fruit of the Spirit.
Your fear cleanses me from the fear of the devil and the fear of men!
By Your fear I defy the devil and all his forces and all his works, so that no evil thought can steal into me, nor idle word, nor wicked conduct!
Your fear is a tree of life, whose branches extend to my emotions and senses and words and conduct.
I pluck from it, and I am sanctified within and without.
I pluck from it Your love, and I love all mankind, even those who oppose me!
v You made with me a wonderful covenant of love, which You recorded in Your holy book.
You gave me Your book to meditate in, and my soul is filled with Your sweetness!
Your commandments are the precious jewelry that adorns my soul!
Your commandments prepare me for the eternal wedding.
My soul sits as a queen adorned with Your commandments, and the heavenly ones marvel at her!
For every perfection I have seen an end, but Your commandments are exceedingly broad.
Since You presented Yourself to me as a heavenly friend, You gave me Your wisdom and Your fear and Your commandment!
How can I suffer isolation, when You accompany me throughout the journey of my sojourn?
How can I complain of my poverty and need, when I am rich in You!
v Glory to You for Your companionship with me, so that I turn neither to the right nor to the left.
My heart will not know duplicity, for it is in Your hand.
Your love fills my whole heart, so the devil will find no place in it!
Glory to You, O All-wise, Giver of holy fear, and Your commandment full of sweetness!

Appendix to Sirach 1 The fear of the Lord The fear of the Lord is manifested in obedience to His commandments, and he who keeps His commandments enjoys inner glory, and lives in the joy and gladness of the Spirit, and receives a crown of rejoicing. Some claim that God's commandments and judgments humiliate man, because they have not experienced the truth of the commandments, which restore to man the image of God so that he becomes in His likeness, and so lives in joy.
The goal of the commandment is that God may dwell in us and in our midst (Zech 2:5). Therefore the fear of the Lord is glory and pride and gladness and a crown of rejoicing.

"The fear of the Lord was created with the faithful in the womb" [12]. Thus the parents' care for their children begins before their birth. For when Zacharias the priest and Elizabeth were sanctified, and St. Mary visited them and brought the incarnate Word, the child John leaped and ran rejoicing in the Lord, and enjoyed the fear of the Lord while still in the womb.
a. There is a relation between wisdom and the fear of the Lord. Both bring happiness and blessing. The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom and its fulfillment and its crown [12, 16, 18].
b. Wisdom is a mother and bride to him who fears the Lord: "She will meet him as a mother, and receive him as a wife married in her youth" (15:2).
c. The eyes of the Lord are upon him who fears the Lord: "And He knows every work of man" (15:19).
d. Those who fear the Lord are filled with blessings and hope: "The fear of the Lord is like a paradise of blessing" (40:27).
e. Those who fear the Lord and the word of God: "They that fear the Lord will not disobey His words" (2:15).

The possibilities of him who fears the Lord: "He that fears the Lord shall fear nothing, and shall not be afraid, for He is his hope" (34:14). "There shall no evil happen to him that fears the Lord; but in temptation He (the Lord) will deliver him again and again. A wise man hates not the law, but he that makes a show of keeping it is like a boat in a storm. A man of understanding trusts in the law, and the law is faithful to him, for it is a divine revelation" (33:1-3).
f. The honor of him who fears the Lord: "What seed is honorable? They that fear the Lord" (10:19).
g. The fear of the Lord is the pride of the elders: "Much experience is the crown of old men, and the fear of the Lord is their glory" (25:6).
h. The fear of the Lord surpasses every good: "The fear of the Lord surpasses all things" (25:11).
i. A good wife is a gift to those who fear the Lord: "A good wife is a great portion, and shall be given to him that fears the Lord" (26:3; cf. 27:3).

entries.section: Between those who fear the Lord and the wicked

paragraphs.text: "He that fears the Lord will receive instruction, and they that seek Him early shall find favor. He that seeks the law shall be filled with it, but the hypocrite will stumble at it. They that fear the Lord shall find judgment, and shall kindle righteous works as a light. A sinful man will not be reproved, but finds an excuse according to his will" (32:14-17).

entries.section: The fear of the Lord and economic life

paragraphs.text: 1. He speaks to us of riches and poverty; riches are good for him who is holy, and poverty is hateful in the mind of the wicked (cf. 13:23). Riches give a man authority and self-confidence, but not like the fear of the Lord and good counsel.

"Gold and silver make the foot stand sure, but counsel is esteemed above them both. Riches and strength lift up the heart, but the fear of the Lord is above them both. There is no loss in the fear of the Lord, and it needs not to seek help" (40:25-26). 2. The rich and the poor: "The rich man does wrong, and yet he proves himself the one wronged, while the poor man is wronged, and is obliged to apologize" (13:3).

He warns us of the importance of work in the spiritual and economic life even to old age: "Hate not laborious work, especially husbandry, which the Most High has created... Have you cattle? Look to them" (cf. 7:15, 22). "My son, lead not a beggar's life; for it is better to die than to beg. When a man looks to the table of another, his living is not to be counted for a life. He loses his self-respect by another man's food, but a man who is wise and well instructed will guard against it. In the mouth of the shameless begging is sweet, but in his belly there burns a fire" (cf. 40:28-30). 3. He warns us of just weights and measures: "A merchant will hardly keep himself from doing wrong, and a huckster shall not be freed from sin" (cf. 26:20). 4. True wisdom and work without planning: "Strive not in a matter that concerns you not, and sit not with sinners in their judgment. My son, meddle not with many matters, for if you multiply them, you shall not go unpunished; and if you pursue them, you shall not overtake them, nor escape by fleeing. There is one that labors, and takes pains, and makes haste, and is so much the more in want" (cf. 11:9-11). 5. The right use of money: "Watching for riches consumes the flesh, and the care of it takes away sleep... The rich man toils in gathering money together, and when he rests, he is filled with his delicacies. The poor man toils in lack of living, and when he rests, he becomes needy. He that loves gold shall not be justified, and he that follows corruption shall be filled with it... It is a stumbling block to them that sacrifice their lives to it, and every fool shall be taken by it. Blessed is the rich man that is found without blemish, and has not gone after gold" (cf. 31:1, 3-5, 7-8).

entries.section: Let us begin with the primary fear

paragraphs.text: v No one can attain to perfect fear unless he first has the primary fear. For the wise Ben Sirach says: "The beginning of wisdom is the fear of the Lord... the crown (head) of wisdom is the fear of God" (Sirach 1:12, 16), meaning by the word "head" the primary fear, which is followed by the perfect fear of the saints.

The primary fear depends on the state of our spirit, and it keeps the soul from every fall, for it was said that by the fear of the Lord everyone departs from evil. But the man who is rid of evil because of his fear of punishment is like a slave who fears his master, and gradually he begins to do good willingly.

In the beginning he works as a hired servant who awaits his wages for his good work. If he continues thus, avoiding evil because of fear like a slave, doing good in the hope of receiving the reward like a hired servant, then he abides in doing good and gains a particular taste for spiritual good, so that he no longer wishes to be separated from it. Then he reaches the work of a son, and loves good for the sake of good itself; and though he fears, he works because he loves. This is the great, perfect fear.
Father Dorotheus

entries.section: The fear of the Lord and the ladder of the life of faith

paragraphs.text: St. Philoxenus presents to us the ladder of the practical life of faith, beginning with its three steps: faith, simplicity and the fear of the Lord. There is no fellowship with God without faith, and faith cannot stand except through the simplicity that God gave to the soul so that it might meet Him as a simple child who believes in his father and clings to him. This simplicity that begets faith is what preserves it, so that the soul, by the grace of God, continues firm in its faith.

Through this faith the soul enjoys the fear of the Lord. It believes in Him and perceives His greatness, and so it fears Him, honors Him, and keeps His commandments. Faith, then, begets "the fear of the Lord"; so the believing man keeps the commandment and obeys it out of fear of punishment... and as he grows by grace he obeys the commandment as a son who fears to wound his father's feelings... He fears that his nature, which he holds in the image of his God and Savior, may be disfigured.

entries.section: 1. He who fears the Lord in the crucible

paragraphs.text: 1 My son, if you come to serve the Lord God, stand fast in righteousness and godliness, and prepare your soul for temptation. 2 Direct your heart and endure. Incline your ear and receive the words of reason, and make not haste in time of calamity. 3 Wait patiently for what you wait for from God; cleave to Him and do not turn aside, that you may be increased in life at your latter end. 4 Whatever comes upon you, accept it, and be patient in the changes of your lowly estate, 5 for gold is tried in the fire, and acceptable men in the furnace of humiliation. 6 Believe in Him, and He will help you. Order your ways aright and hope in Him. Keep His fear, and abide in it until your old age.
My son, if you come to serve the Lord, prepare your soul for temptation [1].
The word son (or child), teknon, occurs 36 times in this book.

"My son": Sirach regards his school as a family that has its role in the life of society. So he calls his disciples "his sons," at times in the plural, a sign of the unity of the disciples with one another and of his relation to them as a father, and at times he speaks in the singular, "my son," to bring out the personal side of each one of them. Sirach wishes to walk in the spirit of God, who deals with the community, whether leaders or people, as all being the people of God, the object of His special love and care. At the same time he sees in each son a particular member who has his own place in his father's heart.

Sirach presents two complementary ideas: that wisdom shows itself in the service of the Lord, and also that it is impossible to attain wisdom without long-suffering in temptations. These two ideas never leave Sirach's thought.

The subject of "temptations" in the life of the young must be discussed, for it is fitting for the young man to learn in some detail not only about the blessings promised to those who strive to please the Lord, but also to know that temptations accompany him during his striving. He must know beforehand what may befall him. This is what the Apostle James affirmed in his epistle: "Behold, we count them happy which endure. You have heard of the patience of Job, and have seen the end of the Lord; that the Lord is very pitiful, and of tender mercy" (Jas 5:11), referring to what befell righteous Job.

After the wise man has linked wisdom with obedience to the divine commandment and the enjoyment of the fear of the Lord, he assures us that the way of God's wisdom exposes us to temptations. Truly the cost of the way is many troubles, but it brings with it surpassing blessings (Sir 4:17-18; 6:24-31).

The Lord did not hide this truth from us, but said to His disciples: "Go your ways: behold, I send you forth as lambs among wolves" (Lk 10:3). He also said: "But before all these, they shall lay their hands on you, and persecute you, delivering you up to the synagogues, and into prisons, being brought before kings and rulers for My name's sake. And it shall turn to you for a testimony... And you shall be betrayed... and some of you shall they cause to be put to death. And you shall be hated of all men for My name's sake" (Lk 21:12-13, 16-17). And the Apostle James says: "My brethren, count it all joy when you fall into divers temptations; knowing this, that the trying of your faith works patience" (Jas 1:2-3). It was also said: "Fear none of those things which you shall suffer: behold, the devil shall cast some of you into prison, that you may be tried; and you shall have tribulation ten days" (Rev 2:10).

In the days of Ben Sirach, opposition to faith in God was centered on the spread of Hellenistic paganism, which crept even into the temple in Jerusalem and reached its height in the days of Antiochus Epiphanes (the antichrist of the Old Testament). Whoever wished to abandon Hellenism while holding fast to the Law exposed himself to persecution by the Greek rulers.

For the believer these temptations perform a work of purification, just as fire refines gold (Prov 17:3). Trust in God's promises, moreover, brings us into divine help in the midst of affliction (Ps 37:3-6; Prov 3:5-6).

What the Fathers of the Church wish to affirm is that the temptations that God permits to come upon believers do not mean God's anger against them or vengeance upon them, but are a sign of divine love, for their purification and progress and for crowning them with the crown of victory. And if He is angry with them, His anger springs from His fatherly love for them.
v It is clear that You are angry, truly angry as a father who corrects, and not as a judge who condemns [1].

v Those whom God appointed before the foundation of the world to take the image of His only-begotten Son (Rom 8:29), who in particular was pressed in His sufferings as the great cluster of grapes, were, before they drew near to the service of God, enjoying in the world a kind of sweet freedom, like clusters of grapes or olives hanging on the tree. But as it was said: "My son, if you come to serve the Lord, prepare your soul for temptation" (cf. Sir 2:1).
Everyone who draws near to the service of God finds himself in a winepress; he endures troubles, and is crushed and pressed, not to perish in this world, but to flow into the storehouses of God.

entries.section: 1. He who fears the Lord in the crucible

paragraphs.text: The coverings of fleshly lusts are removed from him, like the skin of the grape (when it is pressed)... The Apostle speaks of it: "Put off the old man... and put on the new man" (Col 3:9-10; Eph 4:22). All this is accomplished only by pressing. For this reason the churches of God in this time are called "winepresses" [2].
v Be patient and bear the trials that you meet on your way to reach God, for He receives with thanks those who endure patiently in affliction...

entries.section: 1. He who fears the Lord in the crucible

paragraphs.text: The fire of temptations and difficulties produces men who are strong in faith; it may be painful, but it brings forth the strong, because they rest upon a strong foundation [3].
St. Augustine v (A letter of consolation to a father whose two daughters died, and also his maidservant)

I do not deceive you with flattering words, nor do I pull the ground from under your feet with fawning praise. Rather I say what is good for you to hear: "My son, if you come to serve the Lord, prepare your soul for temptation" (Sir 2:1). "When you shall have done all those things which are commanded you, say, We are unprofitable servants: we have done that which was our duty to do" (Lk 17:10).

entries.section: 1. He who fears the Lord in the crucible

paragraphs.text: Say to God: "The two daughters whom You have taken from me are Your gift. The maidservant whom You have taken for Yourself You also lent me for a time for my comfort. I am not grieved that You have taken them back; rather I thank You that You gave them to me before" [4].

entries.section: 1. He who fears the Lord in the crucible

paragraphs.text: v It must be noted that if the Lord had not begun by fasting, Satan would not have found the opportunity (to tempt Him), according to the saying: "My son, if you come to serve the Lord, prepare your soul for temptation" (Sir 2:1). The Savior's own answer indicates that He was tempted as a man: "Man shall not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceeds out of the mouth of God" (Mt 4:4). Therefore, if anyone does not feed on the word of God, he does not live [5].

entries.section: 1. He who fears the Lord in the crucible

paragraphs.text: St. Jerome v Those who have chosen to live a glorious and blameless life must store up beforehand in their mind sufficient zeal to accomplish it. And let them remember him who said: "My son, if you come to serve the Lord, prepare your soul for temptation. Set your heart aright, and constantly endure" (Sir 2:1-2). But those who have no such zeal, how can they reach the goal set before them? The Lord says: "Or what king, going to make war against another king, sits not down first, and consults whether he be able with ten thousand to meet him that comes against him with twenty thousand?" (Lk 14:31) [6]

v Any matter that happens unexpectedly and is grave drives even the brave to disturbance, and sometimes to unbearable terrors. But if it is mentioned beforehand that it will happen, then expecting it lightens the weight of its attack, and this, I believe, is the meaning of the phrase "I was prepared, and was not troubled."

entries.section: 1. He who fears the Lord in the crucible

paragraphs.text: For this reason the divinely inspired Scripture says to those who seek glory through their holy conduct: "My son, if you come to serve the Lord, prepare your soul for temptation. Set your heart aright, and constantly endure" (Sir 1:2). And it does not speak so as to produce in men laziness and indifference... For this reason the Savior of all prepared the disciples beforehand, telling them that He would suffer on the Cross and die in the body once He reached Jerusalem [7].

St. Cyril of Alexandria v When the soul begins to love heavenly realities, and fixes herself strongly on this essential peace, then the ancient enemy, who fell from heaven (Lk 10:18), comes down feeling envy, and begins to multiply his hidden snares.

He develops temptations with greater violence than usual. He tempts all the more the soul that resists. Therefore it is written: "My son, if you come to serve the Lord, prepare your soul for temptation" [1], and be firm in justice and fear [8].
Pope Gregory (the Great)

v God often directs certain kinds of threats that come upon our heads, not in order to bring them down upon us, but in order to draw us to Himself, and when we return to Him the fear quickly dissolves.

Surely, if we remained in the same state during temptations, in tranquility, there would be no need of temptations. And why do I speak of ourselves? Even the saints of old learned a great lesson, for the prophet says: "It is good for me that You have humbled me" (Ps 119:71). And Jesus also said to the apostles: "In the world you shall have tribulation" (Jn 16:33). And Paul refers to this when he says: "There was given to me a thorn in the flesh, the messenger of Satan to buffet me, lest I should be exalted" (2 Cor 12:7)... If we review the whole life of David, we find that he was most glorious when he was in danger, he and those like him.

entries.section: 1. He who fears the Lord in the crucible

paragraphs.text: Such was the state of Job, who shone with the greatest brightness during his troubles. And Joseph also was proved in this way all the more... For all who have worn such crowns of glory gained them by troubles and temptations [9].

entries.section: 1. He who fears the Lord in the crucible

paragraphs.text: v Let us not grieve because of the evils that happen to us. This is soundness of mind. "And make not haste in time of trouble" (Sir 2:2). Many have their manifold sorrows at home, and we share one another's sorrows, even if not from the same source. One is unhappy because of his wife, another because of his child, or his servant, another because of his friend, another because of his enemy, another because of his relative, and another because of a loss that has befallen him. The causes of sorrow are many, so that we find no one free from some kind of toil or misery. Therefore it is fitting for us to be patient, and not to think that we alone are not happy [10].

entries.section: 1. He who fears the Lord in the crucible

paragraphs.text: v There is nothing in moral life that is exempt from sorrow; if not today, then tomorrow, and if not tomorrow, then some day later troubles come. Just as no one can make a long voyage by sea and feel that he is never unsettled, so it is not possible to pass through this life without experiencing sorrow; yes, even for the rich man, since he is rich he will pass through occasions that he does not desire. Yes, even the king himself, for many things govern him, and he cannot accomplish all that he ought to do [11].

v If we sin, God may raise up our enemies against us to discipline us, and therefore we ought not to fight them, but we must examine ourselves and train ourselves. And as long as He has let them loose upon us because of our sins, when we fight them He gives them victory over us. For this reason He commanded us not to repay our enemies. Let us accept trials as we accept medicines from the physician so that we may be saved, and as we accept discipline from the father so that we may be refined. Therefore the wise man said: "My son, if you come to serve the Lord, prepare your soul for temptation" (Sirach 2:1).
St. John Chrysostom Set your heart aright, and constantly endure, and make not haste in time of trouble [2].

Ben Sirach does not ignore human feelings; in time of affliction man suffers and groans, but by faith he cries out to the Lord, and He removes anxiety from him. This is what happened with the Apostle when he cried to the Lord three times to take the affliction from him, and the Lord's answer was: "My grace is sufficient for you: for My strength is made perfect in weakness" (2 Cor 12:9).
When St. John Chrysostom suffered pains and persecution from the Empress Eudoxia, aided by the very men of the clergy, he wrote from his prison to Bishop Cyriacus:
[When I was driven out of the city I was not troubled, but said to myself: If the Empress wishes to banish me, let her do so, for "the earth is the Lord's"!
And if she wishes to saw me asunder, I have Isaiah as an example!
And if she wishes to drown me in the ocean, I think of Jonah!
And if I am cast into the fire, I find that the three youths endured this in the furnace!
If I am put before ferocious beasts, I remember Daniel in the lions' den!
If she wishes to stone me, Stephen, the first martyr, is before me!
If she asks for my head, let her do so, for the Baptist shines before me!
Naked came I out of my mother's womb, and naked shall I leave the world.

entries.section: 1. He who fears the Lord in the crucible

paragraphs.text: Paul reminds me: "If I yet pleased men, I should not be the servant of Christ" [12].]

entries.section: 1. He who fears the Lord in the crucible

paragraphs.text: And St. Cyprian wrote to some confessors, saying to them: ["In all these things we are more than conquerors through Him that loved us" [13].]

v When God wishes to give a man victory and magnify him, He first delivers him to evil (temptations) to be tested and examined, and then He shows his beauty to the world by the blessings that God works with him.

When God wished to give Joseph victory and make him lord over Egypt, what was the beginning of His work to bring him to a good end? First his brothers seized him, and insulted him, and mocked him, and stripped off his clothes, and cast him into the pit, and cut off his hope, and sold him to merchants, and he became a slave serving masters, and the handsome son of free men who had done no wrong was enslaved.

entries.section: 1. He who fears the Lord in the crucible

paragraphs.text: Whoever saw this evil deed could not have thought that all these evils were being done for Joseph's good. But God, who knew what He wished to do for him, had no pity on him when he groaned under the weight of all these evils, but let him fall into the pit, and be sold to merchants, and be thrust into prison unjustly. After all this his beauty shone like the sun, and his right was displayed like gold, and his evils vanished like smoke, and he mounted to the top of the chariot like a king, and rose in the greatness for which God had set him, that he might be humbled and so be exalted [14].

St. Jacob of Serugh v The truly wise man has one concern, which is to obey Almighty God with all his heart and to please Him. And he teaches one thing, only one, which is how to do, as far as he can, what is agreeable to God, thanking Him for His compassionate care, which works in everything that happens in his life.

entries.section: 1. He who fears the Lord in the crucible

paragraphs.text: And just as it is only fitting for us to thank physicians for treating our bodies, even if they give us bitter medicines that are unwelcome, so it is not fitting for us to be ignorant that all things work together for good, by the grace of divine providence, and so deny God's kindness in the things that seem painful to us [15].

entries.section: 1. He who fears the Lord in the crucible

paragraphs.text: St. Anthony the Great v Through divine providence everything is surely good and for the benefit of the soul; all that happens is for our good and our happiness, for God loves us and protects us. As the Apostle says, we must give thanks to God in everything for His goodness toward us (1 Thess 5:18). Let us not sink in our hearts nor lose heart over what happens to us, but accept events, convinced that all that God does with us proceeds from His goodness because He loves us, and all that He does is right. Truly it is impossible for things to go well except through the mercies of God [16].

Father Theodorus of Gaza v Let us drive away from us all worldly cares (anxiety) by prayer and hope. And if we cannot reach this to perfection, let us confess our weakness before God and not cease striving in prayer.
St. Mark the Ascetic Cleave to Him and do not turn aside, that you may be honored at the end of your life [3].

Ben Sirach offers us a practical experience that we benefit from in the midst of affliction, which is that we do not direct our eyes downward lest sorrow swallow us up, but look upward, or into our depths. So we hold fast to the Lord and cleave to Him, and ask for His companionship in the midst of affliction. We rejoice and sing: "I am crucified with Christ: nevertheless I live; yet not I, but Christ lives in me" (Gal 2:20). We enter the narrow way to see eternity cleave to us.

v We know that when a man cleaves to God, He cleanses him to lighten for him the weight of his sins, and the word of the Savior is fulfilled in him: "If you continue in My word, then are you My disciples indeed; and you shall know the truth, and the truth shall make you free" (Jn 8:31-32). For it is God who cleanses man. And it is written that "both He that sanctifies and they who are sanctified are all of one" (Heb 11:2). And also: "Every branch in Me that bears not fruit He takes away: and every branch that bears fruit, He purges it, that it may bring forth more fruit" (Jn 2:15).

entries.section: 1. He who fears the Lord in the crucible

paragraphs.text: My son, cleave to God (Sir 3:2) and flee from all evil works. Help yourself, and flee from sin as one who flees from a serpent [17].

St. Stephen of Thebes v The dispensation of our God and Savior concerning man is to restore man from the fall, and to bring him back from the estrangement that came upon him because of transgression, to direct fellowship with God. Therefore Christ came in the flesh, and lived according to the pattern that we see in the Gospels, and suffered on the Cross and was buried and rose, so that man may be saved by imitating Christ and return to the ancient rank of sonship.

entries.section: 1. He who fears the Lord in the crucible

paragraphs.text: Likeness to Christ alone leads to the perfection of life, not only by being like Him in His life as an example of meekness and humility and patience as a pattern for our life, but also in His death. Therefore Paul, who imitated Christ, says: "That I may be conformed unto His death; if by any means I might attain unto the resurrection of the dead" (Phil 3:10-11) [18].
St. Basil the Great Whatever comes upon you, accept it, and be patient in the changes of your lowly estate [4].

Ben Sirach gives us another exercise, which is to look at the condition of mankind in the world, so that we are like one clinging to the wheel of time. The wheel turns, and we see ourselves at one time above and at another below, at one time in a certain direction and soon in the opposite direction.

The world is changing, but if we are bound to the Holy One, the wheel of time does not occupy us, but the chariot of the Cross, more radiant than the chariot of Elijah the prophet, carries us from glory to glory, until we reach the heaven that awaits us and welcomes us.
v He (the Apostle) says: "Giving thanks always for all things" (Eph 5:20).

What is this? Are we to give thanks for everything that befalls us? Yes, even if sickness or poverty befalls us. If in the Old Testament the wise man counsels us: "Whatever comes upon you, accept it, and be patient in the changes of your lowly estate" (Sir 2:4), how much more in the New Testament?!
Yes, offer thanksgivings even if you do not know the word (that you offer)!...

If you give thanks in rest and prosperity and success and wealth, this is not a great matter, nor is it wonderful; but a man needs to give thanks when he is in sorrows and afflictions and troubles. There is no better word than to say: "I thank You, O Lord"...

Let us thank the Lord for the blessings that we see and those that we do not see, and those that we receive against our will, for we receive many blessings without our wish and without our knowledge...

entries.section: 1. He who fears the Lord in the crucible

paragraphs.text: When we are in poverty or sickness or calamities, let us increase our thanksgivings, and I do not mean thanksgivings in words and on the tongue, but in work and deeds, and in mind and heart. Let us thank Him with all our souls, for He loves us more than our parents do, and as far as evil is from goodness, so great is the difference between God's love for us and our fathers' love [19].

St. John Chrysostom v Know that bodily illnesses are natural to the body, since it is material and corruptible. Therefore if sickness comes upon it, the soul that has learned (goodness) must take courage and endure with thanksgiving, without murmuring against God who created the body for it.

entries.section: 1. He who fears the Lord in the crucible

paragraphs.text: St. Anthony the Great v An elder said of poor Lazarus: "We did not see that he did any virtue, except that he never murmured against that rich man who had no mercy on him, and he was thankful to God for what he had, and for that alone God had mercy on him [20].
From the Paradise of the Fathers: for gold is tried in the fire, and acceptable men (and chosen) in the furnace of humiliation [5].

If the merciful God permitted temptations beyond our power, no man would be able to stand before the cunning schemes of the evil spirits without falling to the ground. The Apostle Paul says: "But God is faithful, who will not suffer you to be tempted above that you are able; but will with the temptation also make a way to escape, that you may be able to bear it" (1 Cor 10:13).

entries.section: 1. He who fears the Lord in the crucible

paragraphs.text: v What if we suppose that a man has fallen into sickness? Well, let him hear another counsel: "In sickness and poverty, trust in (God), for gold is tried in the fire, and acceptable men in the furnace of humiliation" (cf. Sir 2:4-5). Therefore neither death nor loss of money nor bodily sickness, nor insult nor shame nor anything of the kind can grieve him, but makes him more joyful; what ground for sorrow, then, can there ever be? [21]

entries.section: 1. He who fears the Lord in the crucible

paragraphs.text: v We can say: (this) affliction makes those who are troubled more steadfast. "Tribulation works patience; and patience, experience; and experience, hope: and hope makes not ashamed" (Rom 5:3-5). Do you not see that the proof that comes from affliction produces hope in the good things to come, and that steadfastness in temptations causes us hope for the future? For this reason I do not say hastily that these very afflictions point us toward the hope of the resurrection, and put those who are tempted in a better state, since he says: "For gold is tried in the fire, and acceptable men in the furnace of humiliation" (Sir 2:5) [22].
St. John Chrysostom v Hear my prayer, O God, when I am troubled; deliver my soul from fear of the enemy.
The enemies rose up against the martyrs. What was the voice of this Body of Christ (that is, the martyrs) as it prayed?

Was it praying to be delivered from the enemies, and that the enemies should have no power to kill? Were they not heard because they were killed? Did God abandon His servants who had contrite hearts, and did He despise those who had hope in Him? Surely not! For who has called upon God and been forgotten by Him? Who has trusted in Him and been left?
They were heard, and they were killed. Yet they were delivered from their enemies.
Others who were afraid yielded and lived. But these very ones were swallowed up by their enemies.
Those who were killed were saved, and those who lived were swallowed up.

entries.section: 1. He who fears the Lord in the crucible

paragraphs.text: This is what the voice of the recognized Psalmist pointed to when he said: "Then they had swallowed us up quick" (Ps 124:3). Many in truth were swallowed up alive, but many others were swallowed up dead. Those who count Christianity foolishness are in fact dead. There comes a time when they swallow themselves up [23].
St. Augustine Trust in Him and He will help you; order your ways aright, and put your hope in Him. [6]

The Psalmist says: "Our soul waits for the Lord: He is our help and our shield. For our heart shall rejoice in Him, because we have trusted in His holy name" (Ps 33:20-21). No one who trusts in Him is ashamed, for his soul dwells in Him, and God dwells in him (Jn 14:23). "Trust in the Lord, and do good; dwell in the land, and feed on His faithfulness... Commit your way unto the Lord; trust also in Him; and He shall bring it to pass" (Ps 37:3, 5).

v Thus thinks the soul that loves God: God is her place; and she knows no other place to dwell in, and does not dwell in any place except in God, as it is written: "Lord, You have been our dwelling place in all generations." Therefore wherever the true Christian is, he dwells in God, and God dwells in him, and he does not rely on a homeland or a place. For this reason he has no need to move from one place to a similar one. For this I beseech your love to serve your God with divine love, as you are and wherever you may be [24].
St. Jacob of Serugh v He who does not trust in God in small things reveals all the more his lack of faith in great things [25].
v "O Lord my God, in You do I put my trust" (Ps 7:1)...

Although this prayer is simple, and anyone can offer it, it was not offered here in that way. For he who places his trust in a man, or trusts in something else in life, such as authority or possessions, or anything that many regard as glorious, cannot say: "O Lord my God, in You do I put my trust."

In truth there is a commandment that it is not fitting for us to trust in rulers. "Cursed be the man that trusts in man" (Jer 17:5). Just as it is fitting for us not to worship anything besides our worship of God, so it is fitting for us not to trust in anyone other than God, the Lord of all things. It was said: "The Lord is my hope and my praise" (Ps 70:5; 118:14) [26].

v Anxiety expresses the ugliness and weakness of the soul, because of its separation from God. Let us then pray that the light of God's countenance may shine upon us. So we shall be like the saints in their meekness and peace in all circumstances, and always ready to do good, as the Psalm says: "I made haste, and was not troubled" (Ps 119:6); "You have turned for me my mourning into dancing: You have put off my sackcloth, and girded me with gladness" (Ps 30:11).

The joy of God does not settle in all souls, but in those souls that have wept over their sins, with many signs and continual tears, like one who has lost a loved one. Such a soul God turns from mourning into joy. The Lord of glory warns us not to be like children sitting in the market, calling to one another and saying: "We have piped unto you, and you have not danced; we have mourned to you, and you have not wept" (Lk 7:32). The pipe is a musical instrument that gives a note when it is blown, and therefore I believe that every holy prophet is a pipe in the spiritual sense, working by the breath of the Holy Spirit. It was said: "We have piped unto you, and you have not danced," and the words of prophecy urge us to work according to the commandment, which is what is called "dancing."

The prophets weep over us, and call us to weep, so that we may discover our faults in the light of their prophetic words; then we weep over our ruin and subdue our body with striving and punishment. The man who walks in such a way has his sackcloth torn and puts on the adorned wedding garment, so that he is not cast out of the wedding (Mt 22:11-13) [27].

v Question: Does he who was caught in a multitude of evils, and sinned after his baptism, fall into despair of his salvation? Or what is the measure by which a man may still continue in his hope in God's love for mankind through repentance?
Answer: If it were possible to balance God's surpassing compassion or the weight of the greatness of God's mercy against the number and weight of sins, there would be room for despair.

But if it is reasonable that the latter are subject to measure and number, while it is impossible to measure God's mercy or count His compassion, there will never be any room for despair. Rather, by knowing the mercy and condemning the sins, there is forgiveness in the blood of Christ, as it is written (Mt 26:28).

However, there are many places and ways through which we learn that we must not despair. Consider in particular the parable of our Lord Jesus Christ about the son who took his father's wealth and squandered it in sins. From the words of the Lord Himself we learn what kind of feast, and how great, befits repentance (Lk 15:22-24).

Add to this that God says by Isaiah: "Though your sins be as scarlet, they shall be as white as snow; though they be red like crimson, they shall be as wool" (Isa 1:18). But we must know that this is fulfilled only when our repentance deserves it, if it proceeds from our hatred of sin, as it is written in the Old and New Testaments, and bears fruits worthy of it [28].
St. Basil the Great

entries.section: 2. He who fears the Lord is full of hope

paragraphs.text: 7 You that fear the Lord, wait for His mercy, and turn not aside, lest you fall. 8 You that fear the Lord, believe in Him, and your reward shall not be lost. 9 You that fear the Lord, hope for good things, and for everlasting joy and mercy. 10 You that fear the Lord, love Him, and your hearts shall be enlightened. 11 Look at the generations of old, and see; did ever any trust in the Lord, and was ashamed? 12 Or did any abide in His fear, and was forsaken? Or who called upon Him, and was neglected? 13 For the Lord is full of pity and mercy, forgives sins, and saves in time of affliction.

It is fitting for every man to work with all his strength, for he will not achieve what he desires while in idleness; yet what he possesses is from God, like the farmer and the fisherman, each of whom works and the Lord is the one who gives to them.
You who fear the Lord, wait for His mercy, and turn not aside, lest you fall. [7]

Remember that God's dealings through the generations build our faith and our hope on practical experience (Ps 34:8; 37:25). Let us not cast ourselves into the hands of men, but into the hands of God, for His majesty is in His mercy, and His greatness in His compassion.

v Let us learn how to endure without murmuring or objection to what happens to us, for God knows what is good for us. And we must bear calamity with thanksgiving, and then blessings will overtake us. Let us submit to everything that comes upon us, giving thanks to God for everything, for He knows what is good for us better than we know. And He loves us more than father and mother. Let these considerations be a song that we sing to ourselves in time of affliction, so that we may drive out despair and glorify God in everything [29].

entries.section: 2. He who fears the Lord is full of hope

paragraphs.text: St. John Chrysostom You who fear the Lord, believe in Him, and your reward shall not be lost. [8]

entries.section: 2. He who fears the Lord is full of hope

paragraphs.text: You who fear the Lord, hope for good things and everlasting joy and mercy. [9]

The monk Theodore was a friend of St. John Chrysostom in the ascetic life, but the beauty of a young woman of fair appearance named Hermoine led him astray, and he fell in love with her and wished to marry her. Theodore the ascetic fell in love with this woman, but his greatest fall was centered in his despair of God's accepting him and of the possibility of his returning to his former ascetic life. Prayers were offered for him and efforts were made, and finally St. John Chrysostom sent him two letters, which recorded for us the most wonderful remedy that a despairing soul needs, through living hope. They revealed to us God's unlimited mercies and His arms always open to receive sinners and fornicators, however great their sins, with a warning against the most hideous devil, namely the devil of despair.
v Do not despair of your being changed completely.

If Satan has this power, to cast you down to the ground from a towering height and lofty virtue to the utmost limits of evil, how much more is God able to raise you to your former confidence, and make you not only as you were, but happier than before [30].

v Great is the power of hope in the Lord: an unconquerable fortress, a protecting wall that cannot be attacked, an undefeated army reinforcement, a quiet harbor, an impregnable tower, an irresistible weapon, an invincible strength able to discover a refuge in a place no one expects. By this power the unarmed become armed, women fare better than men, and children prove that they easily become stronger than those who practice the arts of war. What wonder if they overcome enemies, when in fact they overcome the world itself... Hope in the Lord changes everything! [31]
v Hope carries us forward. It heals us! Do not be anxious and do not despair, lest your hope become vain [32].

v No one walks in a good life and is anxious about the future... Does our goodness lean on hope? Yes, but not hope in men, which often vanishes and leaves nothing behind but confusion. Our hope is in God, and it is sure and firm [33].

v What does "we are saved by hope" mean? It means that we do not ask for everything for ourselves in this life, and that we have hope also, believing that what God has promised us He will fulfill for us; by this we are saved; for if we lose hope we lose all that we have received...

He wishes to say: I ask, were you not subject to countless sins? Were you not in despair? Were you not under sentence?... What then saved you? Hope in God alone, and your confidence in His promises and gifts, for you have nothing else to offer Him.

If this is what saved you, let us hold fast to it now also. For He who gave you such great blessings cannot deceive you in the blessings to come. He found you dead and broken and a prisoner and an enemy, and made you a friend and a son and free and righteous and an heir with Him, giving you things so great that no one expected them. After enjoying such gifts generously and lovingly, will He betray you in the things to come?...

This way (hope) saved you from the beginning; it is the pledge that you alone brought to the Bridegroom. Let us hold fast to it and keep it, for if you seek anything in this world you lose your goodness by which you became radiant. Therefore the Apostle continues, saying: "But hope that is seen is not hope: for what a man sees, why does he yet hope for?" [34]
St. John Chrysostom v Patience directs us toward hope in things to come, and hope directs us toward the reward [35].

St. Clement of Alexandria v Why do you rely on yourself and fall? Throw yourself on His arms. Do not be afraid. He will not let you slip. Throw yourself in certainty, and He will catch you and heal you.
St. Augustine v Question: How can the soul be fully assured that she is being cleansed from sin?

Answer: If a man knows the motive of David, who said: "I hate and abhor lying" (Ps 119:163; lit. iniquity), or knows that he is fulfilling the commandment of the Apostle who said: "Mortify therefore your members which are upon the earth; fornication, uncleanness, inordinate affection, evil concupiscence, and covetousness, which is idolatry: for which things' sake the wrath of God comes" and adds to this, as an extension of the sentence against every sin, "on the children of disobedience" (Col 3:5-6), so that he can say: "A froward heart shall depart from me: I will not know a wicked person" (Ps 101:4).

Again, a man ascertains that he has such a restraining motive if he bears an emotion with trembling, as the saints do. Therefore David says: "I beheld the transgressors, and was grieved; because they kept not Your word" (Ps 119:158). And the Apostle says: "Who is weak, and I am not weak? who is offended, and I burn not?" (2 Cor 11:29).

Now, if according to the truth of the word the soul is above the body (Mt 10:28), and we care for the body, so that we loathe and hate every filthiness and sympathize and grieve from the heart when we see wounds or harm befalling the body, how much more regarding what befalls sinners. For he who loves Christ and loves his brothers suffers for them when he sees their souls wounded as by ravening beasts, and savagely exposed to the attacks of deadly evil. So David says: "My wounds stink and are corrupt because of my foolishness. I am troubled; I am bowed down greatly; I go mourning all the day long. For my loins are filled with a loathsome disease: and there is no soundness in my flesh" (Ps 38:5-7). The Apostle says: "The sting of death is sin" (1 Cor 15:56).
Therefore when a man knows that his soul has come to be in such a state, because of his sins and the sins of others, he is confident that he is being completely cleansed from sin [36].
v Question: How must a man turn back from sins (Acts 3:19)?

Answer: Through the zeal of David's disposition, who first said: "I acknowledged my sin unto You, and my iniquity have I not hid. I said, I will confess my transgressions unto the Lord" (Ps 32:5); then he declared the state of one who learns to work in various ways in the sixth Psalm and in the other Psalms.

A man may learn from the Apostle those things that he testified to the Corinthians concerning the sin of others, when he said: "Godly sorrow works repentance to salvation not to be repented of" (2 Cor 7:10). And he adds the signs of that sorrow: "For behold this selfsame thing, that you sorrowed after a godly sort, what carefulness it wrought in you, yea, what clearing of yourselves, yea, what indignation, yea, what fear, yea, what vehement desire, yea, what zeal, yea, what revenge! In all things you have approved yourselves to be clear in this matter" (2 Cor 7:10-11).

It is clear from this that it is fitting for us not only to leave sin, and to bear these things on account of sinners, but we must also withdraw from the sinners themselves. David did this plainly when he said: "Depart from me, all you workers of iniquity" (Ps 6:8), and the Apostle commanded us: "With such an one no not to eat" (1 Cor 5:11) [37].
St. Basil the Great Consider the generations of old, and see:
Did any trust in the Lord, and was ashamed?
Or did any abide in His fear, and was forsaken?

entries.section: 2. He who fears the Lord is full of hope

paragraphs.text: Or whom did He ever call upon, and He despised him? [10]
He presents three questions concerning His faithfulness in the generations of old, and with those who trust in Him in the present so that they may enjoy His mercy.

Another exercise in the midst of temptations is the study of God's dealings with believers, whether in the Old Testament or the New Testament or throughout history, as in our own life. The God who kept us in the past keeps us in the present and will keep us in the future. The Apostle Paul says: "Who delivered us from so great a death, and does deliver: in whom we trust that He will yet deliver us" (2 Cor 1:10).

entries.section: 2. He who fears the Lord is full of hope

paragraphs.text: For the Lord is full of pity and mercy; He forgives sins, and saves in time of affliction. [11]
God's attributes here are the foundation upon which man's faith and hope in Him are built.

v We have two parents who bore us on earth for misery, and then we die. But we have found two other parents. God is our Father and the Church is our mother, who bore us for eternal life. Let us consider, beloved, whose sons we have become. Let us walk in a manner worthy of such a Father... We have found for ourselves a Father in the heavens; therefore we must pay attention to our conduct while we are on the earth. For he who belongs to such a Father must walk in a way by which he deserves to receive his inheritance [38].

St. Augustine v This is the work of God... God created the heavens and the earth and the sea. Great are these works and worthy of His wisdom! But none of these has the power to draw human nature to Him like His mercy and His love for mankind! [39]
St. John Chrysostom

entries.section: 3. He who fears the Lord escapes three woes

paragraphs.text: 14 Woe to fearful hearts, and faint hands, and the sinner that goes two ways. 15 Woe to the faint heart, for it believes not, and therefore it shall not be defended. 16 Woe to you that have lost patience, and have forsaken the right ways, and turned aside into crooked ways, 17 and what will you do when the Lord shall visit?
He who fears the Lord escapes the three woes that befall him who fails in courage, simplicity of heart and patience.

Woe to cowardly hearts and slack hands; and to the sinner who goes two ways [12]. 1. The first woe is for the one with the fainting heart who limps between the two ways, so that he is a member of the people of God and at the same time walks in the pagan ways. 2. The second woe is for him who does not trust in God, and so finds no refuge to take shelter in. 3. The third woe is for him who has no hope; what will he do when the Lord visits him with discipline? Here Ben Sirach refers to David, who chose to fall into the hand of the Lord and not into the hand of man (2 Sam 24).

v What does it mean: "Let us draw near with a true heart" (Heb 10:22)? That is, without hypocrisy, for "woe to the fearful heart and the feeble hands" (cf. Sir 2:12). He means: may there be nothing false among us. May we not say one thing and think another, for this is falsehood, and may we not be faint of heart, for this is not the mark of a "true heart" [40].

St. John Chrysostom v When we come to the grace of Baptism, renouncing all other gods and lords, we confess the one God, the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit. But when we confess this, if we do not love the Lord our God with all our heart and all our soul and cleave to Him with all our strength (Mk 12:30; Deut 6:5), we are not the portion of the Lord, but rather are like one set upon a kind of fence, and we suffer from those iniquities from which we fled, and we do not please the Lord to whom we fled and took refuge, because we do not love Him with a whole and sincere heart (Mk 12:30).

For this reason the prophet cries out to us, seeing similar wavering in our hesitation, when he says: "Woe to the sinner who goes two ways"; "How long halt you between two opinions?" (1 Kgs 18:21). And James the Apostle says: "A double minded man is unstable in all his ways" (Jas 1:8). So we who do not follow the Lord with a straight and perfect soul, and move among strange gods, are like one on a fence. On the one hand we behave as one who has left the strange gods who drag us down, and on the other hand our Lord does not protect us because we are unsteady and hesitant [41].

Origen v If someone dies because he was given remedies that depend on superstitions, how many have died because of these remedies? And how many have died without a remedy? With what confidence does his spirit go to God? He has lost the sign of Christ, having exchanged it for the sign of Satan.

Perhaps he will say that he has not lost the sign of Christ. Can you have the sign of Christ together with the sign of Satan? Christ does not accept joint ownership. He wishes to be the sole owner of the one He bought. He bought him at a great price (1 Cor 6:20), to be the sole owner. Will you make Him a partner with Satan, to whom you sold yourself by your sin? "Woe to those of two hearts," who in their hearts offer a portion to God and another to Satan. God is angry that Satan has a portion, and so He leaves (the heart) and Satan reigns over all of it. There is a reason for the Apostle's counsel: "Neither give place to the devil" (Eph 4:27) [42].
St. Augustine Woe to the faint heart, for it believes not, and therefore it shall not be defended. [13]

What does he mean by the faint heart? The heart that loses patience and endurance, and walks with a double mind arising from unbelief or its weakness, so that it becomes unstable in all its ways (Jas 1:8).

v He whose spirit trusts in God cleaves to God. God is faithful, and does not allow him to be tempted above what he is able to bear, but with the temptation makes also a way to escape, so that he is able to endure and does not draw back in the day of battle (1 Cor 10:13).

He who glorifies himself and not God, even if he puts on a great show such as bowing down... yet he tends to draw back and flee from the day of battle. His spirit is not faithful toward God, and therefore the Spirit of God is not with him. It is written: "Everyone who does not believe in the will of God is not defended" (cf. Sir 2:15) [Vulgate] [43].
St. Augustine Woe to you that have lost patience, and what will you do when the Lord shall visit you? [14]

The Lord Christ says: "In your patience possess you your souls" (Lk 21:19). Thus the Lord placed the possession of the soul in the virtue of patience, because patience is the root of all the virtues and their guardian. Patience is to endure calmly the evils that fall upon us from others, without bearing feelings of resentment against the one who brings them upon us.

God permits affliction to believers, but as a Father He declares His care for them, so that not one hair of them perishes; and as St. Augustine says: [Be assured, brethren, that the enemies have no power over believers except to the extent that they are negligent in their temptation and trial [44].] He also says: [When the Lord Jesus urged His martyrs to patience, He promised them that the body itself would receive complete perfection in the future without loss, I do not say loss of a member of it, but without the loss of a single hair [45].]

v One may follow in the Gospel the words of our Lord Jesus Christ: "In your patience possess you your souls" (Lk 21:19). And in another passage of Holy Scripture it was said: "Woe to you that have lost patience" (cf. Sir 2:14). Whether you call it patience or endurance or forbearance, the various expressions point to the same thing.
Let us set an anchor in our hearts, and not be much concerned with the difference of words, but let the single meaning occupy us. May we enter into the depth that the words express.

The person who is occupied with the truth that the life he walks in this world is far from his true home lives in patience wherever he is in the body here on earth. He lives in patience when he knows that he possesses an eternal home in heaven, confident that in this state he finds his happiness, which he cannot find here. He is inflamed with desire for it, and it is a good, holy and pure desire!

It is clear that patience is not necessarily in prosperity but in afflictions. No one can say that he endures patiently what is pleasant; what we bear and sustain by patience is something harsh, something bitter. Patience is not necessarily in happiness, but is exercised in misery [46].
St. Augustine

entries.section: 4. He who fears the Lord and satisfaction with the word of God
