paragraphs.text: 18 They that fear the Lord will not disobey His words; and they that love Him will keep His ways. 19 They that fear the Lord will seek that which is well pleasing to Him; and they that love Him will be filled with the law. 20 They that fear the Lord will prepare their hearts, and will humble their souls in His sight. 21 They that fear the Lord will keep His commandments, and will be patient until His visitation, 22 saying: "If we repent not, we shall fall into the hands of the Lord, and not into the hands of men, 23 for as His majesty is, so is His mercy."
Those who fear the Lord do not disobey His words, and those who love Him keep His ways [15].

The Lord Christ directs His speech to all believers who love Him, and shows that the divine promise is general for all, and He makes of the heart a divine dwelling or temple. "If a man love Me, he will keep My words: and My Father will love him, and We will come unto him, and make Our abode with him. He that loves Me not keeps not My sayings: and the word which you hear is not Mine, but the Father's which sent Me" (Jn 14:23-24).

v He says: "Fear God, and keep His commandments" (Eccl 12:13). Thus by keeping God's commandments you will be strong in every work, and every work will be beyond all criticism. Therefore fear the Lord, and you will do every work well; this is the fear that you must possess in order to be saved.
Do not fear Satan. By your fear of the Lord you gain authority over the devil, and he has not the least power...
In any case, fear the works of Satan, and do not carry them out, but be on your guard against them.

There are two kinds of fear (the fear of the Lord, and the fear of Satan or of men); if you wish to do evil, fear the Lord and do not do it. Accordingly the fear of the Lord is a guarantee and power and glory. Fear the Lord and live for Him. All who fear Him and keep His commandments will live for Him [47].
Father Hermas v The proof of love is its declaration through work. This is the reason why John says in his epistle: "He that says, I know Him, and keeps not His commandments, is a liar" (1 Jn 2:4).
Our love is true if we keep our will in harmony with His commandments. He who wanders here and there through his evil lusts does not truly love God, for he opposes God in his will [48].
Pope Gregory (the Great)

v Remind yourself that you must always show your prudence, through a good life and your very deeds. In the same way the sick respect physicians and look upon them as their rescuers and benefactors by deed and not by word [49].
St. Anthony the Great Those who fear the Lord seek His good pleasure, and those who love Him are filled with the Law. [16]

St. Philoxenus presents to us the word of God as a living source of the divine fear, enjoining us not to repeat it with our tongue only, but to live it in our hearts, so that divine springs burst forth within us that water the soul and turn its wilderness into a fruitful paradise.

v Let us be occupied always with the word of God, not only by repeating it with our tongues, but also by meditating on it inside our hearts, so that the tongue may speak out of the abundance of the heart...
He who is continually watered by the divine teaching yields divine fruits at all times.
The hidden secrets of the heart are declared, and appear through the conduct of the other senses and their actions [50].

St. Philoxenus v If anyone does not keep His commandments, this is evidence of his lack of love for God and His Christ; but keeping the commandments of Christ by enduring temptations even to death is the proof of love (Jn 14:21, 24; Rom 8:35-37) [51].
v God honors and glorifies him who does His will, but him who disobeys His law He dishonors (Mt 5:6; Rom 2:23) [52].

v "O taste and see that the Lord is good" (Ps 34:8)... He who has not tasted honey cannot perceive its flavor. So the word of God cannot be enjoyed by teaching alone, but we must experience the depth of the teachings of truth, and touch the love of the Lord in a personal relationship. He says: "Taste," and he did not say be satisfied, "for now we see through a glass, darkly" (1 Cor 13:12), but a time will come in which I possess what I now receive as a pledge.
By grace I can taste it with this taste in fullness of joy.

Those who cannot taste foods, and have no appetite for them, but turn away from all food with disgust, ought to present themselves to the physician, so that he may open their appetite with appetizing foods, with the addition of foods of pungent (smell) to open their appetite more and more. So it is with the word of truth: we need a living experience of it, as the Psalm says that it will kindle in you a constant desire; therefore it says: "Taste," that you may receive the blessing, from your constant sense that you "hunger and thirst after righteousness" (Mt 5:6) [53].
v Question: What is the measure of our love for God?
Answer: That the soul be enlarged beyond her strength toward the will of God, and make His glory her chief concern and constant desire [54].
v Question: How can we do everything to the glory of God?...
If we do everything according to the mind of God and His commandments, and do not seek the praise of men [55].
St. Basil the Great Those who fear the Lord prepare their hearts, and humble themselves before Him. [17]

St. Jacob of Serugh says that the enemy, the devil, and Adam fell into the same vice, that is, pride; therefore God took away Adam's glory lest he fall forever like Satan, and the Lord Christ repaired the situation by our acquiring His humility, so that His Kingdom may dwell in us.
v That compassionate One, full of good things, had pity with mercies, and took from (Adam) the glory in which he was clothed.
He stripped from him the glory in which he was robed, lest he be proud and perish finally like Satan.
He used rebuke with him as He despised him: O son of dust, you are dust and a lowly clay.
Why do you wish to snatch a place that is not yours?...
You did not stretch out the heavens alone, nor did you set in order the powers that go about in them.
The sun and the moon and all the stars do not move by you...
You are dust, do not reach for greatness; you are clay, why do you think on what does not concern you?...
Hate pride, for it is a great snare, full of death, in which the enemy fell from the beginning...
There is nothing so hated and rejected with God as the pride of him who struts in boasting [56].

St. Jacob of Serugh v The low lands are filled, and the high lands dry up. Grace is rain. Why then do you wonder if God resists the proud, and gives grace to the humble (Jas 4:6)? Therefore the saying "with fear and trembling" (Phil 2:12) means with humility. "Be not highminded, but fear" (Rom 11:20). Fear so that you may be filled; do not be proud lest you dry up! [57]
St. Augustine Let us fall into the hands of the Lord and not into the hands of men, for as His majesty is, so is His mercy [18].

St. John Chrysostom sees that David, the king and prophet, when he sinned and deserved discipline, asked the Lord that he might fall into His hands and not into the hands of men, because He is a merciful God, who knows what is for his edification and the edification of the people, and does not exaggerate the discipline. He is a wise, almighty and loving Father! But if he fell under the hand of a man, this man in arrogance does not aim at his correction, and does not seek what is for his edification and the edification of the people.

But on the great day of the Lord, the falling of the obstinate man who has determined not to repent until the last breath of his life into the hand of the Lord is exceedingly terrible (Heb 10:30), and then falling into the hands of men is counted as nothing.

v He says: "It is a fearful thing to fall into the hands of the living God" (Heb 10:31); it is written: "Vengeance belongs unto Me, I will recompense, says the Lord" (Heb 10:30)... It was said: "Let us fall into the hands of the Lord and not into the hands of men" (Sir 2:18; 2 Sam 24:14). But if you do not repent, you fall into the hands of the fearful God, and falling into the hands of men is counted as nothing. He means: when you see a man punished here, let us not be terrified by present things, but be terrified by the things to come." As His mercy, so also is His wrath" and "His indignation comes upon sinners" (Sir 5:6) [58].

St. John Chrysostom v For those who have newly entered the way of godliness, the chief exercise for their greater profit is "fear," according to the counsel of Solomon, the wisest of men: "The fear of the Lord is the head of wisdom" (Prov 1:7). But as for you who have passed your infancy in Christ, and no longer seek milk, but are able to become perfect in the inner man by the food of strong teaching (Heb 5:13-14), that is, you need the high commandments by which all the truth concerning love in Christ is fulfilled.

But you must be fully careful lest through the abundance of God's gifts you fall under a severe judgment, if you are ungrateful to the Giver (God), for He says: "For unto whomsoever much is given, of him shall be much required" (Lk 12:45) [59].

v Yes, the Lord is good, but He is also just, and it is a property of the just to repay according to desert... The Lord is merciful, but He is also fair, for it was said: "The Lord loves mercy and judgment" (Ps 100:1) [60].
v He is merciful, but He is also a judge, for the Lord "loves mercy and judgment," as the Psalmist says...
You see how wisely He grants mercy; but He is not merciful without justice, nor just without mercy, for the Lord is merciful and just (Ps 115:5) [61].

v The people murmured because there was no water. As soon as Moses said to his people: "Must we fetch you water out of this rock?" (Num 20:10), he hesitated to some degree, but for this alone he immediately received the threat that he would not enter the Promised Land, which was at that time the head of all the promises given to the Jews. When I see this man ask and not obtain pardon, when I see him not found worthy to receive forgiveness for these few words, besides so many works of righteousness, I truly perceive the severity of God in the words of the Apostle (Rom 11:22). I perceive fully that these words are true: "If the righteous scarcely be saved, where shall the ungodly and the sinner appear?" (1 Pet 4:18) [62].

St. Basil the Great Holy Scripture brought out the wrath with which God threatens mankind, not so that we may live in terror, but that, as children of God, we may perceive the blessings that we enjoy by returning to Him.

v When we read of the wrath of the Lord and His anger, we must not understand the word according to the sense of an ignoble human emotion, but in a sense that befits God, who is above every passion or blemish. Hence we must perceive from this that He is the Judge and the Avenger of all the unjust things that are committed in this world.

And by the logic of these terms and their meaning, we must fear Him as the One to be feared who repays us for our works, and we must fear to do anything against His will. For human nature is accustomed to fear those whom it knows to be angry, and is alarmed at offending them, as is the case with some judges who have reached the height of justice.

The avenging wrath is usually feared by those who are tormented by the accusation of their consciences, though of course not because this inclination exists in the minds of those who will adhere to fairness in their judgments. But while they are in the midst of this fear, the judge's inclinations toward them are marked by justice and impartiality and respect for the law that he carries out. And this, however gently and kindly he acts, is branded with the harshest epithets of anger and fierce wrath by those who were punished rightly and fairly [63].

St. John Cassian v You find many passages in Holy Scripture in which God is likened to the attributes of man. So if you ever hear the words "the wrath of God and His fury," do not think that wrath and fury are emotions and attributes that exist in God, but they are a way by which God condescends and speaks to discipline His children and correct them.

For we also, when we wish to direct our children and correct their faults, appear before them in a fearful form and with a stern and firm face that does not correspond to our true feelings, but corresponds to the method of discipline.

If we showed on our faces always the forbearance and leniency that is in our souls and inner feelings toward our children, without changing the features of our faces according to the children's behavior, we would spoil them and reduce them to the worse. In this way we speak of the wrath of God; when it is said that God is angry, what is meant by this wrath is for your repentance and your correction, because God in His truth does not become angry or furious, but you are the one who will bear the effects of wrath and fury when you fall into terrible, severe torments because of your sins and evils, when God disciplines you with what we call the wrath of God! [64]

Origen v "We were by nature the children of wrath, even as others" (Eph 2:3). And Jeremiah says of this wrath: "Cursed be the day wherein I was born" (Jer 20:14). And of this wrath the blessed Job says: "Let the day perish wherein I was born" (Job 3:3). Of this wrath Job himself says again: "Man that is born of a woman is of few days, and full of trouble. He comes forth like a flower, and is cut down..." (cf. Job 14:1-5).
St. Augustine

entries.section: Practical exercises

paragraphs.text: Ben Sirach presents to us the following exercises during affliction: 1. To prepare ourselves for temptations, asking God to fix His fear in us [1], and to believe in the heavenly Savior, that He is kinder and more loving than our parents, and that He is almighty and wise. 2. To resist anxiety in distress by crying out to God [2]. 3. To fix our eyes on God and not on the temptation [3]. 4. To look at temporal life as ever changing [4]. 5. To look at God's dealings with His believers throughout history and in our own private lives [10].
Inspired by Sirach 2

entries.section: Let me fall into Your hands, and not into the hands of man!

paragraphs.text: v My soul praises You and thanks You when You allow me the crucible of temptations!
You bring me into the fires of affliction, but with Your surpassing love You surround me.
With the three youths I experience the fires of the furnace, which have become dew!
Through affliction You open my insight, and I see the glory that You prepare for me!
v Your grace sustains me, and fills my depths with hope in You!
Afflictions turn into crowns of eternal glory!
In the midst of the furnace You hear the hidden thanksgivings of my heart, and You join me to the chorus of the heavenly ones.
Instead of anxiety, my soul rejoices in You, O my Savior!
v Three gifts I ask of You in my affliction.
Give my heart the spirit of strength, so that it does not faint, nor limp between two ways!
Draw me to Your pierced side, and I shall take refuge in You!
Give me heavenly wisdom, so that I may perceive what is beyond the affliction, and my faith does not weaken, nor do I lose patience, and so I become one of Your beloved in whom You delight.
v Grant me, with David the prophet and king, to cry out to You:
Let me fall into Your hands, and not into the hands of man (2 Sam 24:14).
You are truly my Father and my Savior and my only Friend.
If my father forsakes me and my mother forsakes me, You take me to Yourself!
You penetrate my heart, and You know its possibilities and its secrets.
You will not permit affliction unless it is for the edification of my soul and for the profit of many.
You are all-wise; all that You permit is for my salvation and the salvation of my brethren.
By Your fiery Spirit You continually renew my nature; You pour out Your radiance on my depths in the midst of the fires of temptations.
You shape my depths, and I become a living icon of You.
You adorn me, and the heavenly orders take pride in Your work in me.

entries.section: 1. Fatherhood and sonship in the Lord

paragraphs.text: 1 The sons of wisdom are the assembly of the righteous, and their offspring are the people of obedience and love. 2 O my children, hear the words of your father, and do them, that you may be saved. 3 For the Lord has honored the father over the children, and has confirmed the judgment of the mother over the sons. 4 He who honors his father atones for his sins, and refrains from them, and is heard in the prayer of every day. 5 And he who respects his mother is like one who lays up treasures. 6 He who honors his father rejoices in his children, and in the day of his prayer he is heard. 7 He who respects his father will have long days, and he who obeys his father gives rest to his mother. 8 He who fears the Lord honors his parents, and serves his parents as masters to him.

When he speaks of the holy family, he regards his school as a family that has its role in the life of society. He calls his students his sons, at times in the plural, a sign of the unity of the students with one another and of his relationship to them as a father, and at times he speaks in the singular: "My son." He desires to walk in the Spirit of God, who deals with the community, whether leaders or people, as all being the people of God, the object of His love and special care. At the same time he sees in each son a special member who has his own special place in his father's heart.
He also made clear the secret of the concern for fatherhood or motherhood and sonship:

a. "And do what I tell you, that you may be saved" [1]. The love translated into fatherhood and sonship is the way of salvation. For the heaven prepared for us has love as its law, and whoever does not practice love for God and people does not enjoy it.

entries.section: 1. Fatherhood and sonship in the Lord

paragraphs.text: b. This love is in truth a divine commandment; every honor given to parents the Lord counts as honor given to Himself, and it is a right that they receive through the divine commandment [2].

entries.section: 1. Fatherhood and sonship in the Lord

paragraphs.text: c. Every honor directed to them opens for us the door of God's mercies, so that we receive forgiveness of our sins, and every care for the mother and glorification of her is a credit for the son or daughter, kept as a treasure in heaven [4].

entries.section: 1. Fatherhood and sonship in the Lord

paragraphs.text: d. What we offer to our parents is repaid to us later by our children, and it lifts up our prayers here, while we are in the world, as on two wings to heaven [5].

e. Whoever honors his parents, the Lord blesses every minute of his life, so his life is lengthened through the divine blessing, and the Lord makes each day of his days as a thousand years (2 Pet 3:8).

f. It befits children not to be ashamed of serving their parents; whoever honors his parents according to the flesh is counted as an offering to the heavenly Father and to the Church, his spiritual mother, and therefore he serves them as masters to him.
In brief, the Lord Himself looks upon the family as the church of the holy home.
He also made clear the secret of the concern for fatherhood or motherhood and sonship:
My children, listen to me, your father, and do what I tell you, that you may be saved [1].

When Sirach calls himself a father to his students and regards them as his sons, he only affirms that the constitution of the family rests on mutual love and on concern for the salvation of all its members. What concerns him is not that they should occupy distinguished positions in society, nor that they should be trained to conduct dialogues in a certain manner, but that all should work for salvation.

* The Lord taught us not only to take no thought about anything concerning our possessions and the necessities of this life, but also to rise above natural feelings, when He said: "He that loveth father or mother more than me is not worthy of me" (Mt 10:37). This applies also to deep ties such as close friendships. How much more, then, to distant relations and to those who are strangers to the faith. Therefore He added: "And he that taketh not his cross, and followeth after me, is not worthy of me" (Mt 10:38). The Apostle, who succeeded in this, writes to us: "the world is crucified unto me, and I unto the world... I live; yet not I, but Christ liveth in me" (Gal 6:14; 2:20).

Let us return to the words of the Lord that He spoke directly to each one of us. When that man asked Him, saying: "Lord, suffer me first to go and bury my father," He answered him: "Let the dead bury their dead: but go thou and preach the kingdom of God" (Lk 9:59-60). And that other who said to Him: "Lord, I will follow thee; but let me first go bid them farewell, which are at home at my house," He answered him with rebuke and reproof, saying: "No man, having put his hand to the plough, and looking back, is fit for the kingdom of God" (Lk 9:61-62)...

He wants us to refrain from hearing any voice that makes us turn aside from the way of perfection and godliness... For He says: "Whosoever doth not bear his cross, and come after me, cannot be my disciple" (Lk 14:27). We do this when we pass through the waters of Baptism, where we declare our faith and confess that we were crucified with Christ and died and were buried with Him... as it is written (see Rom 6:4-11)[1].
St. Basil the Great For the Lord honored the father over his children, and confirmed the right of the mother over her sons [2].
Whoever honors his father atones for his sins [3].
And whoever glorifies his mother is like one who lays up treasures [4].
Whoever honors his parents expects God to hear his prayer, just as he expects that his children will honor him.
Whoever honors his father will rejoice in his children, and when he prays he is heard [5].
When the Holy Bible speaks of the father, it usually means the parents; there is no distinction between fathers and mothers.

entries.section: 1. Fatherhood and sonship in the Lord

paragraphs.text: Whoever exalts his father will have a long life, and whoever obeys the Lord gives rest to his mother [6].

entries.section: 1. Fatherhood and sonship in the Lord

paragraphs.text: The Holy Bible links obedience to the Lord with obedience to parents. By honoring our parents we receive the blessing of obedience to the divine commandment (Deut 28:1-2). Kindness to parents helps in the forgiveness of sins, and contempt for parents is counted as blasphemy against God [16].

Obedience to parents does not stop at children and youth, for it also befits the person who reaches adulthood to honor his parents, and so receive the blessing of the Lord. At the same time his work returns to him, as his children honor him and obey him. It is stated in this book:
And serves his parents as masters to him [7].
Those who fear the Lord serve their parents with joy. It befits them to help them in their old age and to be gentle with them if they lose their reason.

entries.section: 2. The blessing of obedience and honoring parents

paragraphs.text: 9 Honor your father in deed and word, with all patience, 10 that a blessing may come upon you from him, and his blessing remain to the end. 11 For the blessing of the father establishes the houses of the children, and the curse of the mother uproots their foundations. 12 Do not glory in the dishonor of your father, for the dishonor of your father is no glory to you, 13 but a man's glory is the honor of his father, and the disgrace of the mother is a reproach to the children.
Honor your father in word and deed, that a blessing may come upon you from him [8].

Every honor that a person gives to his parents is counted as seed that he sows, to reap it later. This commandment is the only one stated among the Ten Commandments together with the blessings that it carries. "Honour thy father and thy mother: that thy days may be long upon the land which the LORD thy God giveth thee" (Ex 20:13).

The Holy Bible gave attention to this divine commandment, to which a divine promise is attached, so Ben Sirach cites it here [8-11] at some length, perhaps because some young people were drawn by philosophy away from attachment to the Law, so they despised the older generation, especially their parents, and considered themselves more advanced and more knowledgeable.

In the New Testament the Apostle Paul cited the same commandment: "Honour thy father and mother; which is the first commandment with promise; that it may be well with thee, and thou mayest live long on the earth" (Eph 6:2-3). And after the Flood, the first curse that fell upon man in the new world was because of Ham's dishonor of his father Noah (Gen 9:20-27).

The Jewish rabbis say, in commenting on the commandment "Honour thy father and thy mother," that before the Babylonian captivity the relationship between parents and children had in general worsened, so that Israel deserved to fall under captivity because it did not keep that commandment, which is tied to a long stay in the Promised Land. And the New Testament conveys to us a sorrowful picture of this denial on the part of children, for in the Gospel of our teacher Matthew it is stated: "Whosoever shall say to his father or his mother, It is a gift, by whatsoever thou mightest be profited by me; and honour not his father or his mother" (Mt 15:5). And in the Gospel of our teacher Mark: "If a man shall say to his father or mother, It is Corban, that is to say, a gift, by whatsoever thou mightest be profited by me; ye suffer him no more to do ought for his father or his mother" (Mk 7:11-12). This tradition is commandments of men, contradicting the divine commandment for one purpose or another, like the example that the Lord Christ gave. For the sake of personal benefit the Jewish leaders laid down a commandment bearing the appearance of outward giving while hiding a breaking of the divine Law. For instance, a son could deprive his parents of their rights, not supporting them under the pretext that what he would pay them he offers as an offering to God, so he breaks the commandment of honoring parents, and is like one who cursed them by his deeds, and this is harsher than reviling with the tongue, for he deprives them of the right to a dignified life, and brings them into hardship of living under the cover of giving to the Temple. As Origen says: [When the fathers hear that what should be given to them has become part of the offering devoted to God, they refrain from taking it from their sons, even if they are in great need of the necessities of life.] And he says: [That the Pharisees were lovers of money (Lk 6:14), so they pretended to collect it to give to the poor, depriving the parents of the gifts of their children.]
For the blessing of the father establishes the houses of the children, and the curse of the mother uproots their foundations [9].

entries.section: 2. The blessing of obedience and honoring parents

paragraphs.text: Do not glory in the dishonor of your father, for the dishonor of your father is no glory to you [10].

* "Do not glory in the dishonor of your father" (3:10). If this is said about our fathers according to nature, how much more about our spiritual fathers. Honor him because he serves you every day, and makes you read the Holy Bible, prepares the house for you, and guards you, and prays for you. He intercedes before God on your behalf, and offers supplications for you; all his worship is for your sake. To value all this, think on this, and draw near to him with godly reverence.

Do not say: He is wicked... The gifts that God gives are not based on the virtue of the priest. All His gifts are from His grace. The role of the priest is merely to open his mouth, and God is the One who does everything[2].
St. John Chrysostom Fulgentius feared that virgins might fall into pride and haughtiness toward their families because of their virginity.

* Just as lust has no power over the body of a virgin, so do not give pride power over the heart of a virgin. Work out your salvation in fear and trembling. For God works in you, that you may will and do His good will.
Fulgentius (a disciple of St. Augustine)

entries.section: 2. The blessing of obedience and honoring parents

paragraphs.text: But a man's glory is the honor of his father, and the dishonor of the mother is a disgrace to the children [11].

entries.section: 3. Bearing with the weaknesses of parents

paragraphs.text: 14 My son, help your father in his old age, and do not grieve him in his life. 15 And if his mind fails, bear with him, and do not despise him while you are in your full strength, for mercy shown to a father will not be forgotten. 16 And by bearing with the failings of your mother you will be repaid with good. 17 And upon your righteousness a house will be built for you, and you will be remembered in the day of your affliction, and like ice in fair weather your sins will be dissolved. 18 Whoever forsakes his father is like a blasphemer, and whoever provokes his mother is cursed by the Lord.

If one of the parents is afflicted with the weakness of old age, or with illness, or with loss of memory, the son regards this as by God's permission, so instead of murmuring he shows compassion to them. This tenderness has its effectiveness:
a. Sirach says of it that it is not forgotten [14]; it is a credit for the son with God, who hastens his deliverance in time of affliction.
b. It helps the son to atone for his sins; Ben Sirach likens it to the sun that melts the ice in fair weather.
My son, help your father in his old age, and do not grieve him in his life [12].
In an agricultural society the son can contribute to the work of sowing, as well as to tending the sheep.
And if he loses his mind, show compassion, and do not despise him while you are in all your strength [13].
For kindness to a father is not forgotten, and it counts toward atoning for your sins [14].

entries.section: 3. Bearing with the weaknesses of parents

paragraphs.text: The day of your affliction will be remembered to your benefit, and like ice in fair weather your sins melt away [15].

When Ben Sirach spoke of the blessings of honoring parents, he lifted our hearts to God our heavenly Father, that we may enjoy His surpassing care. We honor our heavenly Father by offering Him a sacrifice of thanksgiving, especially in time of affliction, a sign of our faith and our trust in His care for us in the midst of affliction. The fruit of this thanksgiving is that it helps us to atone for our sins, that we may live by the righteousness of Christ.

"The day of your affliction will be remembered to your benefit, and like ice in fair weather your sins melt away." What a joyful comparison, for thanksgiving in affliction brings us into the clear light of day, and the Sun of righteousness melts our sins and removes them.
* What shall I render to You, O Lord? For when my memory recalls these things (the afflictions), I shall not be frightened by them!
I love You, O Lord, and I thank You, and I confess to Your name!
For You remove from me my evil, terrifying and malicious deeds.
I ascribe to Your grace and mercy that You melt my sins like snow[3].

St. Augustine St. Augustine sees our sins as resembling the ice that melts and dissolves by the work of the Holy Spirit. [We became frozen in captivity, our sins bind us, but when the south wind (the warm one) blows, that is, the Holy Spirit, He forgives our sins, and we come down from the ice of iniquity. For just as snow melts in warm weather, so also do our sins.[4]]

entries.section: 3. Bearing with the weaknesses of parents

paragraphs.text: Whoever forsakes his father is like a blasphemer, and whoever provokes his mother is cursed by the Lord [16].

entries.section: 4. The family is a school of meekness

paragraphs.text: 19 My son, conduct your affairs with meekness, and the good man will love you. 20 The greater you are, the more humble yourself, and you will find favor with the Lord. 21 For the power of the Lord is great, and by the humble He is glorified. 22 Do not seek what is too hard for you to attain, nor search out what is beyond your power, but what God has commanded you, meditate upon it, and do not desire to investigate His many works. 23 For you have no need to see hidden things with your eyes, 24 and what goes beyond your works, do not be overly concerned with it. 25 For you have been shown many things that exceed the understanding of man. 26 And many have been led astray by their presumption, and a corrupt fancy has made their minds slip. 27 The hard heart will end in evil, and he who loves danger will fall into it. 28 The heart that goes in two ways will not prosper, and the perverse of heart will stumble in both. 29 The hard heart is burdened with hardships, and the sinner adds sin to sin. 30 The disease of the proud has no cure, for the root of evil has taken root in him. 31 The heart of the intelligent ponders a proverb, and the desire of the wise is a listening ear. 32 The wise and intelligent heart refrains from sins, and prospers in works of righteousness.

When the Word of God became incarnate and dwelt among us as one of us, He called us to learn from Him, saying: "Learn of me; for I am meek and lowly in heart" (Mt 11:29). Marriage and family life rest on the divine plan, and on the realization of God's plan for family life and for each member of the family. Through holy family life in the Lord, society comes to walk in harmony with God's plan, fulfilling its mission.
Ben Sirach gives us practical touches for a life of meekness and humility, for the believer to live in his small family as well as in society, which is the greater family.

entries.section: 4. The family is a school of meekness

paragraphs.text: The most beautiful offering with which parents are pleased is the humility and meekness of their children. The more the son humbles himself in his conduct toward them, the more he grows in greatness in the eyes of God and people. God is glorified in the humble person, because he knows his weakness and trusts in God, who raises up the weak as a hero (see Joel 3:10). The believer does not seek visions and the working of wonders and miracles; what concerns him is walking according to the divine commandment [21-22].

entries.section: 4. The family is a school of meekness

paragraphs.text: As the eye must be opened in order to receive the light [25], so the mind ought to be opened to receive wisdom (Prov 28:14).
a. Meekness does not stop at certain words or particular behaviors, but ought to be blended into and shine forth in all the works of the believer [17].

b. The believer does not seek worldly honor, but whenever he receives honor or authority or success in his works he ought to grow in humility, counting what he receives as free gifts from God, so he finds favor with the Lord, and honor even from people [18].

c. The believer ought not to think of himself more highly than he ought to think (Rom 12:3), but to recognize the truth of his abilities and capacities. So he does not seek what is beyond him, nor search into hidden matters through useless theoretical, disputatious dialogues [21-24]. When Pope Athanasius was asked by a person to show him his God so that he might believe in Him, he answered him: "Show me your spirit, and I will show you my God!"
d. Beware of falling into intellectual stubbornness.
My son, conduct your affairs with meekness, and the people whom the Lord approves will love you [17].
The greater you are, the more humble yourself, and you will find favor with the Lord [18].

If the fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom, then arrogance is the beginning of folly. Ben Sirach had in mind what pride had done, not only to individuals but also to nations, for Assyria fell, then Babylon, then Persia. He also lived through the fall of Carthage in 201 BC.

Humility is the disposition fitting for those who fear the Lord, who honor their parents. The more a person receives honor, whether on the ecclesiastical or the worldly level, the more he needs to double his humility, so that he may become the object of God's pleasure and not of people's approval. The archbishops used to fear pride lest they lose their salvation. So St. John Chrysostom would repeat in the depths of his heart, as among the bishops, his famous saying: "I marvel at a bishop who is saved!" At the beginning of the celebrations of the ordination of Pope Shenouda, he would sometimes open his speech by repeating what Chrysostom said, so that words of praise might not distract him from his eternity. The saying of our beloved father Fr. Bishoy Kamel is: The servant of church education is the servant of the children of his Master, and the priest is the servant of the servants, the children of their Master; how much more must this be the feeling of the bishop and the patriarch.
What grieves our hearts is that a priest thinks he is the head of the Church and that what he says must be obeyed without dialogue, and likewise the bishop and the patriarch.
* Often the ecclesiastical order and the Levitical work are a cause of falling into pride for one who forgets that he received this honor in the bosom of the Church.

How many men of the priesthood, when they became head, forgot that they must be humble, as though their ordination had exempted them from humility. On the contrary, they must keep humility carefully, because they are granted such great honor, according to the saying of Scripture: The greatest among you, let him be the most humble.

The community chooses you, so bow your head in greater humility. It has chosen you as a leader of others, so do not feel that you are glorified! Be among them as one of them (Lk 22:27). You must be humble and meek. Flee from pride, the source of all evils[5].

* The evil one fights us not only that we should commit sin with persistence..., but that we should be proud and feel that we are perfect. But God resists the proud and gives grace to the humble (Prov 34:3; Jas 6:4; 1 Pet 5:5). Therefore the more you humble yourself, the more you are lifted up and find mercy with God [18]...

Whoever turns aside from the commandment does not follow it, since the commandment of God is upright. "Cursed are they that turn aside from thy commandments" does not refer only to those who do not work them, but even to those who deviate from them a little.

Origen * "LORD, my heart is not haughty, nor mine eyes lofty: neither do I exercise myself in great matters, or in things too high for me" (Ps 131:1). Let us say this more clearly, and be heard. I am not proud. I did not wish to be known among people for wonderful powers, and I did not seek anything beyond my strength. In this I boast among the foolish... May no man be proud of God's gift to him, but keep humility, and so fulfill what is written: "The greater you are, the more humble yourself, and you will find favor with the Lord" [18]. How much fear is needed of pride in God's gift. We must press ourselves more and more[6].

St. Augustine * Let our glory be in humility, and our boasting in not loving (vain) glory. And let our desire be in those things that please God and satisfy Him, keeping in our minds what the Wise Man says to us: "The greater you are, the more humble yourself, and you will find favor with the Lord" (Sir 3:18). For He rejects the proud, and regards the arrogant as His enemies. But the meek and the humble in heart He crowns with honors[7].
St. Cyril the Great For the power of the Lord is great, and the humble glorify Him [19].
Do not seek what is too hard for you, nor search into what is beyond your power [20].

Pride reaches its extreme when a person becomes arrogant through his philosophical studies, and does not take into account that the gift of the mind is from God. With all its wonderful greatness, he realizes that it is limited and cannot come to know the mysteries of the Unlimited, nor His plan, without enjoying the work of His divine grace.

It befits us to seek wisdom and to grow in the knowledge of it, without relying on mere rational thought, for God, who treasures man as His ambassador on earth, does not withhold knowledge from him, but offers him what is for his edification according to man's capacities, and also reveals to him His divine will.

The danger that Sirach feared was that there had seeped into the holy land a disregard for the word of God and an indifference to the will of God, through Hellenistic ideas. This atmosphere created Jewish leaders who were arrogant in their thoughts and conduct.
* Deep meditation on the good life and care for the soul beget good people who love God.
Whoever seeks God finds Him, by overcoming all lusts through constant prayer. Such a person does not fear the demons[8].
St. Anthony the Great St. Ambrose presents Arius as an example of one who claims to be possessed of knowledge in what goes beyond human ability.

* It was said to Arius and to all men: "Do not seek what is far too hard for you." Moses was forbidden to see the face of God (Ex 33:23), and Arius thought he was qualified to see Him in a mystery... Paul speaks of lower matters: "For we know in part, and we prophesy in part" (1 Cor 13:9). But Arius says: "I know God with full knowledge, and not in part." Thus Paul is less than Arius. The chosen vessel knows in part, and the vessel of destruction knows all. Paul says: "I knew a man... whether in the body, I cannot tell; or whether out of the body, I cannot tell: God knoweth; how that he was caught up into paradise, and heard unspeakable words" (2 Cor 12:3-4). Paul was carried up to the third heaven and did not know himself, while Arius wallows in filth and knows God.
Paul says of himself: "God knoweth," and Arius says of God: "I know"[9].
St. Ambrose Meditate on what you have been commanded, for you have no need of hidden things [21].

* The Holy Bible warns us: "Meditate on what you have been commanded, for you have no need of hidden things" [22]. "Do not seek what is too hard for you, nor search into what is beyond your power" [21]. Of course we cannot use words that ascribe vain curiosity to the Holy Spirit. We must only say that searching into the hidden matters of God is a portion of his nature[10].

St. Epiphanius, Bishop of Salamis * Do not seek what is too hard for you, nor search into what is beyond your power [20]. This does not mean that these matters are forbidden to us, for the Lord says: "There is nothing covered, that shall not be revealed; and hid, that shall not be known" (Mt 10:26). But if we continue in the way we have undertaken, as the Apostle tells us, God will not only reveal to us what we do not know and ought to know, but will reveal whatever we care to know (Phil 3:15).

The way we have undertaken is the way of faith. May we keep it without hesitation. May it bring us into the mysteries of the King, in whom are hid all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge (Col 2:3)...

It befits us to proceed in progress and growth until our hearts become qualified and receive what we are unable to receive now. And if we find, on the last day, that we have advanced sufficiently, then we shall learn what we cannot know here[11].
St. Augustine Do not meddle in (searching) what goes beyond your works, for what has been revealed to you exceeds the understanding of man [22].
What is it that goes beyond your work? Searching into what cannot be comprehended, such as the essence of God or even the essence of the human soul.

* We read in Isaiah about Christ: "Who shall declare his generation?" (see Isa 53:8). When the blessed prophet speaks of God the Word, he uses the word "generation" instead of saying "essence" or "being." In truth, who can declare the being of the Only-Begotten Son? And what language can explain the unspeakable begetting of the Son from the Father? And what mind does not stand helpless and powerless before this concept? In truth we know and believe that the Word was begotten of God the Father. But we say that to entertain any question about this matter in discussion is extremely dangerous... We must not search into matters that exceed our mind and knowledge, not for us alone but for every creature, including those who are spirits[12].

St. Cyril the Great * God has not made all things revealed to you, nor has He permitted all things to be unknown to you. For He does not permit all things to be unknown to you, lest you say that the things that exist are not from (divine) providence. Nor does He permit all things to be known to you, lest the greatness of your knowledge stir up pride in you. So, at least, the wicked Satan pushed the first man to recklessness through the hope of greater knowledge, stripping him of the knowledge that he already had. Therefore the Wise Man advises us, saying: "Do not seek what is too hard for you, nor search into the things that exceed your power, but meditate with reverence on what you have been commanded, for the greater part of His works are done in secret" (see Sir 3:21-22)[13].

* "What has been shown to you exceeds the understanding of man" (Sir 3:22). But he says this for the consolation of the grieving, rebellious man, because he does not know everything. For even these things that (man) observes, and which he is permitted to know, are far greater than your understanding, since you could not attain them by yourself, but God taught them to you. Therefore be content with the wealth (in knowledge) that has been given to you and do not ask for more; rather give thanks for what you have received, and do not be angry about the things you have not received. Give glory for what you know, and do not stumble because of the things you do not know. For God made both equally profitable, and He reveals some things and hides others for the sake of your peace[14].
St. John Chrysostom Many have been led astray by their conclusions, and their evil suppositions made their thoughts slip and fall [23].
The stubborn heart ends in ruin, and he who loves danger perishes in it [24].

Fulgentius sees that the Wise Man is speaking here of the stubborn heretic, so he calls him to return to the Catholic Church, in which is the love that covers a multitude of sins through the gift of the Holy Spirit.
* Question: If one will fall under many blows, while another under few blows (Lk 12:47), how do some say that the punishment is infinite?

Answer: The things that were said in a veiled and obscure manner in certain places of the inspired book of God have been made clear in explicit terms in other places. The Lord declares once that these go away into eternal punishment (Mt 25:46), and again that He sends persons to the everlasting fire prepared for the devil and his angels (Mt 5:22), and adds: "Where their worm dieth not, and the fire is not quenched (Mk 9:48), which the prophet said rightly long ago: "their worm shall not die, neither shall their fire be quenched" (Isa 66:24).

Since many such sayings are found everywhere in the inspired Holy Bible, this is certainly one of the strategies of Satan: that many people, by ignoring these valuable and weighty words and declarations of the Lord, reassure themselves that the punishment has an end, so that they may commit sin with great boldness. If there were an end to eternal torment, then surely life would not be eternal.

Now if we cannot bear to think in this way about eternity, by what logic is it possible to give eternal torment an end? The attribute "eternal" is attached equally to both elements. Therefore He says: "And these shall go away into everlasting punishment: but the righteous into life eternal" (Mt 25:46).

From the viewpoint of the explicit sayings, we must understand that those who are beaten with many blows, and those who are beaten with few blows, this does not mean an end to the torment, but points to different degrees.

If God is a just Judge, not only for the righteous but also for the wicked, who "will render to every man according to his deeds" (Rom 2:6), therefore one deserves an unquenchable fire, which can burn quietly or slowly, and another may deserve the worm that dieth not, and this can be moderate or great according to exactly what the person deserves.

A third may deserve Gehenna, in which there is a different kind of torment, while another deserves outer darkness (Mt 8:12; 22:13; 25:30), where all he does is weep, and another suffers gnashing of teeth because of excruciating pain. And outer darkness certainly indicates that there is also an inner darkness.
Moreover it is said in Proverbs about the depths of hell (Prov 9:18), which shows that some of those in hell are not in its depths, but receive less torment instead.

This can be clarified now by taking into consideration the condition of the body. One may suffer from fever with other symptoms and pains, while another suffers from fever but not like the former. And in another way a third, who differs from the first person, does not suffer from fever, being sick, but has pain in his limbs, which may be greater or less.

Now in the present case the "much" and "few" that the Lord spoke follow the customary style with different expressions. And for us this manner of speaking is applied to one afflicted with some illness, as we say in wonder concerning a person who suffers only from fever or from a sharp pain in his eyes: how long has he been suffering, or what troubles he suffers.
Again I say that punishment, severe or mild, is not related to the lengthening or shortening of time, but to the difference of the punishment[15].
St. Basil the Great The stubborn heart is burdened with pains, and the sinner adds sin to sin [25].

entries.section: 4. The family is a school of meekness

paragraphs.text: The disease of the proud has no cure, for the plant of evil has taken root in him [26].

Ben Sirach affirms the danger of stubbornness, which touches the depths of man before it appears in behavior; he attributes it to the heart as well as to the mind. If the fruit of stubbornness is ruin and deviation from sin to sin, he counts it as the root of a hidden plant which inevitably yields its bitter fruit in due time, and without ceasing. This stubbornness has no cure by a mere human decision to stop it, but needs grace, able to change and renew the thick and hardened heart (Mk 8:17; Heb 4:7).

The intelligent man reflects on the discourses of the wise, and makes his ears attentive to the voice of the Lord, so he enjoys with Moses the prophet the divine presence when he drew near to the bush burning with fire and not consumed, and through this presence came to know the mystery of the incarnation of the Word of God. The wise man sings in the spirit of humility with the Psalmist, saying: "LORD, my heart is not haughty, nor mine eyes lofty: neither do I exercise myself in great matters, or in things too high for me. Surely I have behaved and quieted myself, as a child that is weaned of his mother: my soul is even as a weaned child" (Ps 131:1-2).

* I am not proud: I do not wish to be known among people for wonderful powers, and I do not seek anything beyond my ability, of which I boast among the foolish. Like Simon the Magician, who wished to advance in wonders beyond his abilities, and therefore was the more pleased with the authority of the Apostles than with the righteousness of Christians[16].
St. Augustine The heart of the intelligent reflects on the proverb[17], and the attentive ear is the desire of the wise [27].
Have you cattle? Look to them, and if they are profitable to you, keep them [22].

The faithfulness of the wise man does not stop at the members of the family, or friends, or people in general, but extends to caring for the animals that he owns (Prov 27:23-27; Deut 25:4; Prov 12:10).
Have you children? Instruct them, make them obedient from their youth [23].

If the Lord calls us to care for animals, how much more must we care for our brothers among men. The Apostle Paul says: "Doth God take care for oxen? Or saith he it altogether for our sakes?" (1 Cor 9:9-10). The aim of discipline is that the children be marked by a spirit of obedience, so that they become like the Lord Christ when He was a boy, for He was obedient to St. Mary and Joseph the carpenter.
Have you daughters? Take care of their chastity, and do not show yourself too lenient toward them [24].

He who loves his daughter does not pamper her in a way that makes her lose concern and care for her chastity, but spares no effort that she may live pure until the day of her marriage. Some have been known for excessive pampering of their children, especially the wealthy, which spoils the happiness of the children themselves and deprives them of fulfilling their mission. Others have been marked by great harshness, especially where there are family problems. Therefore, firmness should be joined with tenderness, and with gentleness and tenderness firmness should be observed in moderation.

Some see that the care for daughters here is as for weak vessels, so that the parents do not put them to work that might rob them of their freshness and youth, which would affect them at their marriage. As for not being cheerful before them, perhaps what is meant is not to spoil their modesty by gatherings in which conversations take place that offend their modesty [20].
St. John Chrysostom warns the shepherds of the Church against pampering girls out of pity, lest the girls misunderstand the shepherds [21].

v Christ, the Educator of humanity, the divine Logos, calls us to spare no effort, with all strength and together with the gift of wisdom, to save our children by rebuke, discipline, calling them to account, warning them, and offering the remedy together with promises and gentleness toward them...
In short, God deals with us so that we ourselves may deal in this way with our children.
Have you children? Instruct them... Our children, whether male or female, you should love above everything else [22].

v In truth the Teacher of humanity, the divine Word, devotes Himself with all His power to save His little ones by every means through the plan of His wisdom: by warning, reproach, rebuke, correction, healing, promises, and giving benefits... In truth God deals with us as we deal with our children: we care for their bodies, and we do not show ourselves too lenient toward them. Yet we cherish a great love for our children, sons or daughters, more than love for anything else [23].
St. Clement of Alexandria: Marry your daughter, and you will have done a great thing, but give her to a man of understanding [25].
Have you a wife after your heart? Do not divorce her, but do not trust yourself to a wife whom you hate [26].

He did not command the husband to love his wife, but indirectly made clear that his not loving her represents a danger to him. If the Law permitted divorce because of the hardness of their hearts, so that the husband would not act rashly toward his wife, here Ben Sira warns the husband against divorcing his wife out of his desire for a woman more beautiful than she. For the highest beauty is in wisdom, understanding, godliness, and good management. But if the husband feels that his wife is unfaithful, let him beware of her lest she deceive him and turn toward evil.
Honor your father with all your heart, and do not forget your mother's pains in childbirth [27].
Remember that you were born of them; and what will you repay them for what they have done for you? [28]

There is no one who wishes for a person good, progress, and success more than they do. God granted the mother to labor with joy and delight for the sake of her children. God presents her love for her children as a likeness of His watchful care over us: "Can a woman forget her sucking child, that she should not have compassion on the son of her womb? yea, they may forget, yet will I not forget thee" (Isa 49:15).

entries.section: 6. Uprightness of life and honoring the priests of the Lord

paragraphs.text: 31 Fear the Lord with all thy soul, and reverence his priests. 32 Love him that made thee with all thy strength, and forsake not his ministers. 33 Fear the Lord, and honour the priest. 34 And give him his portion, as it is commanded thee; the firstfruits, and the trespass offering, 35 and the gift of the shoulders, and the sacrifice of sanctification, and the firstfruits of the holy things.

The discussion of man's relation to the priests of the Lord comes after the discussion of family life. This reveals the concept of the priesthood, whether in the mind of the priest or in the mind of the people.

One of the bishops of the Church of England asked me about the reason for the attachment of the youth in Egypt to the Church and the growing desire for consecration to the Lord, whether through the diaconate, the priesthood, or monasticism. My answer was: the first reason is our view of the priesthood. The believer looks upon the priest as a member with him in the same family, opening to him everything that touches his life as a son to his father. And the priest does not feel that he is an employee who demands an annual leave and is sent into retirement. For although it is the right of his family and his own right to spend a special period with the family, it is not as a personal right that he asks for it, but for the building up of himself and his family.
How my soul grieved when I called the pastor of the church in Los Angeles and said to him: "Reverend," and he answered me: I am now "Mr." because I have been retired!

The priest, even on his deathbed, intercedes for his people as his children, and even when he departs to Paradise he presents his children to the Lord that He may bless them and work in their lives. For this reason it is fitting for us to join what Sirach said, "uprightness of life and honoring the priests of the Lord," to the previous section concerning uprightness of family life.

Honoring the priest is realized in his imitation of the Lord Christ, "who washed the feet of His disciples," and in his sharing with his Church family, and indeed, if possible, in sharing the sufferings of every person. The greatness of the priest is not in an authority he demands, but in his attachment to the heavenly High Priest, who cares for the salvation of mankind and lifts them up to the heavenly mind.
Fear the Lord with all your soul, and honor His priests [29].

Ben Sira cared for the life of the Church, liturgical worship, and honoring the priests. He praised Aaron, the first high priest, as he praised the high priest of his own time, Simon son of Onias. The Lord did not will to give them a special portion in the Promised Land, but wished to distinguish them by being Himself their portion.

Ben Sira emphasized the obligation to give the priests their dues, because the spread of Hellenistic culture and the attraction of some to pagan philosophies had an effect on the priests' income, and some of them were compelled to work in farming.
Love Him who made you with all your strength, and do not forsake His ministers [30].
Fear the Lord and honor His priests, and give him his portion, as you have been commanded:
from the firstfruits, and the trespass offering, and the gift of the shoulders, and the sacrifice of sanctification, and the firstfruits of the holy things [31].

v He who honors the priest honors God also, and he who learns to despise the priest, in the course of time blasphemes God. He says: "Honor My priests" (see Sir 7:31). The Jews learned to despise God because they despised Moses and wanted to stone him. So he who moves with godliness toward the priest does this all the more toward God. And if the priest is wicked, God, when He sees you honoring him although he is not worthy of honor, rewards you for your honoring him [24].
St. John Chrysostom

entries.section: 7. Divine love and our responsibility toward the forgotten

paragraphs.text: 36 And stretch thine hand unto the poor, that thy blessing may be perfected. 37 A gift hath grace in the sight of every man living; and for the dead detain it not. 38 Fail not to be with them that weep, and mourn with them that mourn. 39 Be not slow to visit the sick: for that shall make thee to be beloved.

It is indeed good for a person to be generous with everyone, and to take part in burying the dead (Tob 1:17). Ben Sira also calls us to share the grief of the sorrowful and to visit the sick (Rom 12:15; Mt 25:39-40). Finally, a person's knowing that he is mortal keeps him humble (7:17; 28:6), along with offering due honor to one's neighbor.
Stretch out your hand to the poor, that your blessing may be perfected [32].

The Holy Bible cares for the forgotten groups who have no one to ask about them, and it requires kindness even toward the dead and the sick, so that the believer may bear witness to unbelievers that God is "the God of the forgotten, the suffering, the needy, and the oppressed." Let the believer's hand be stretched out in giving, and his heart in love toward unbelievers, as an ambassador of God, the Lover of mankind.
v [On the widow's mites and almsgiving]

Her love was greater than her offering, for love is better than whole burnt offerings... Therefore she overcame the rich with her offering. The priests of the people receive vows from those who offer abundantly, while the Lord of the priests sat down in a humility they did not perceive. The greedy chief priests care for sacrifices, but our Lord sought love within the soul... The Son of God rejoices in the one in whom there is love.
v The widow was able to know that the Most High has no need of an offering, but seeks a reason to enrich them.

She thought that if He had wished, He would have turned the dust into gold and the waters of the sea into coral, and she said to herself that He does not ask for gold out of need, but that people may share with Him by their offerings. For gold and silver are His, and as it is written, if the sacrifice is great and the love of the one who offers it is small, He rejects it. This woman alone knew how to discern and to offer with a pure heart a complete vow, with discernment... With pure love she knew how to offer! She offered her complete vow better than Jacob. For she did not set apart a tenth of her possessions, but this blessed woman loved the Lord more than herself!
St. Jacob of Serugh: Let her show the tenderness of giving in the presence of all the living; even to the dead let her not withhold kindness [33].

What does he mean by kindness to the dead? Caring for burying them with fitting honor, as Tobit used to do; caring for their families if they had debts; and giving alms to those to whom the dead man was kind.
Do not withdraw from those who weep, and grieve with the sorrowful [34].

The Apostle Paul says: "Rejoice with them that do rejoice, and weep with them that weep" (Rom 12:15). It may be easy for a person to grieve with the grieving and groan with his groaning, but it is hard for some to rejoice with the joy of their brother. This requires a lofty soul, so that he does not envy his brother for his success, but rejoices with him, counting every success of his brother as success for himself. The Apostle says: "And whether one member suffer, all the members suffer with it; or one member be honoured, all the members rejoice with it. Now ye are the body of Christ, and members in particular" (1 Cor 12:26-27).

St. John Chrysostom says: [Nothing establishes love so strongly as sharing in joy and sorrow. Because you are far from troubles, do not isolate yourself also from sharing with others. When your neighbor is in distress, count the distress as your own. Share his tears to support his contrite spirit, and share his joy so that the joy in him may become deep and rooted. Establish love, for by this you serve yourself more than you serve him. By your tears you become merciful, and by feelings of gladness you purify yourself of envy and gloom... If you cannot remove the evils from him, share with him by your tears, and you remove half of the evil; and if you cannot increase his good things, share his joy, and you add to him something great [25].]
Do not hesitate to visit the sick, for by such visits you will be beloved [35].

The Lord Christ counts the visiting of the sick as a visit to Himself, for He says: "I was... sick, and ye visited me" (Mt 25:36). As we desire the healing of the sick, it is fitting for us to desire for him also the fellowship of the eternal glories at the proper time.

entries.section: 8. Divine love and eternal glory

paragraphs.text: 40 In all your works, remember your latter end; you shall never sin forever.
In all your affairs remember your latter end, and you will never sin [36].

The believer in all his works speaks of nothing, and nothing occupies his heart, so much as his entering into heaven. He becomes like Aaron the high priest, upon the skirts of whose robe round about golden bells were fastened. "And it shall be upon Aaron to minister: and his sound shall be heard when he goeth in unto the holy place before the LORD" (Ex 28:35). So in every work he practices and in every matter he thinks about, what occupies him is his meeting with the Lord and his standing before the divine throne in the heavenly sanctuaries, where he enjoys the eternal glories and is in the company of the heavenly ones and in the fellowship of praise with them.

v Let him also have bells around the hem of his garment, for Holy Scripture says: when he enters the sanctuary he gives a sound and does not enter in silence (see Ex 28:35). These bells, which give a sound, were placed on the hem of the garment. Their purpose, as I believe, is that you must not be silent about the last things and the end of the world, but you must ring the bells continually and converse and speak according to what was said: "Remember your latter end, and you shall never sin" (Sir 7:36) [26].

Origen v says: "Remember your latter end, and you shall never sin" (Sir 7:36). For He who now forgives our sins will judge our sins on the day of judgment. He who died for us will appear again to judge all mankind [27].

St. John Chrysostom v [Speaking of Marcella]: "Remember your latter end, and you shall never sin" (7:36). This is like the precept of the sarcastic writer: "Live with death in your mind, and time flies"... She spent her days and always lived thinking that she would certainly die. Her very garments were as if reminding her of the tomb. And she offered herself a living sacrifice, reasonable, acceptable to God (Rom 12:1) [28].
St. Jerome v Question: How can we do everything for the glory of God?...
If we do everything according to God and His commandments, and do not seek the praise of men [29].

v "Arise, O Lord my God... in the commandment that You have commanded" (see Ps 7:8). This saying can also point to the mystery of the Resurrection, since the psalmist calls upon the Judge to arise to take vengeance on every sin and to fulfill the commandments that He had set for us... Do not take vengeance for me, but for Your commandment which You commanded, and they despised it" [30].
St. Basil the Great: Inspired by Sirach 7

entries.section: Our heavenly Friend and brotherly love

paragraphs.text: v With the boldness of love Moses refused to move unless You, O Lord, went before the whole procession Yourself, for he said: "If thy presence go not with me, carry us not up hence" (Ex 33:15).
And behold, I call You, O my Savior, not only to accompany me, but to dwell within me.
Your presence, O my holy Friend, turns my depths into Your holy Kingdom.
It inflames my heart with longing for continual departure toward heaven with joy and exultation.
Your presence fills my depths with love for all my brothers, the sons of men.
By Your dwelling within me, I will not accept evil, and all iniquity departs from me.
The enemy of good cannot enter into my heart, my mind, and all my depths, and he will not dare to take hold of the steering wheel, for it is in Your hand!
v I will not desire a high position, nor temporal glory. And I will not boast of righteousness.
For everything that is holy is a gift from You, O righteous and holy One.
And if I fall into sin, You raise me up by Your fiery Spirit, and fortify my life so that I do not return to it.
My longsuffering heavenly Friend, I know Your forgiving mercies.
Behold, I ask for Your grace to fashion me, so that I may truly become a living icon of You!
v O You who accept gifts and offerings though You have no need of them. You call me: "My son, give me thine heart."
Receive my heart, and I will converse with You with an open heart. And let my prayer and all my worship ascend like the fragrant smell of incense, a place of Your delight and pleasure.
Let my prayer rise like a fire blazing with love.
And I will not cease giving, returning to You from what You have given me!
v Receive, O heavenly One, all my life and my movements, and allow me to walk in the steps of Your footprints.
In You I will not mock any person, whatever his weaknesses, for he may rise by Your grace, and I may fall through my foolishness!
I cherish Your friendship with me, O Truth, so that the devil, the father of liars, may have no authority over me!
v I will keep silence, especially in the presence of experienced elders.
Even in prayer, what concerns me is not much speaking and eloquence, but the language of the heart, unheard by men.
v I hope that I will not cease working even in my old age and sickness, for You do not take rest in the idle.
I will flee from the gatherings of sinners, where there is no place for You among them!
I will go about with You doing good, and I will gain friends for myself always!
v Enter, O heavenly Beloved, my house and dwell in the midst of the family.
My family is called by Your name, for I am Yours, my Beloved, and You are mine!
Be manifested in the life of the whole family, the old and the young.
Grant all love, wisdom, discernment, and prudence.
So that every member may desire to offer honor to the rest of the members!
v Grant me the spirit of simplicity, that I may see You in every priest and servant in Your Church!
v Let those whom You love be beloved to me.
I will care for the poor as Your little brother, and for the needy, the suffering, and the oppressed, for You declare that You are the God of the forgotten!
I will seek the lost and the outcast, that I may see You bring them back to Yourself and embrace them.
v Be with me until the last breath; prepare me before the agonies of death, and in the moments of death, and after death.
Open my insight, that I may see the heavenly sanctuaries awaiting my weakness and all my brothers!
